result.question: Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me) — covering (1) data and information visualization, (2) component and container patterns, (3) new/emerging named visual style movements of 2025-2026 and what now reads as AI-default, (4) motion and interaction for cards/drawers/lists/charts, (5) micro-interactions and micro-animation timing, (6) loading, progress and perceived performance — with primary sources, documented failure modes, and a final mapping to STYLES.md / CRAFT.md.
result.summary: The six areas reduce to two research modes: measured/authoritative knowledge (perception research, WAI-ARIA and NN/g pattern guidance, perceived-performance thresholds) and current-practice/taste knowledge (2025-26 style movements, anti-template discourse, web-native motion implementation). I split along that axis — one query each for dataviz perceptual foundations, the component-pattern and focus-management canon, emerging aesthetics plus the AI-slop critique, native motion/scrollytelling implementation (which carries micro-interaction timing), and the evidence base for loading and perceived performance.

angles.label: academic / perceptual foundations of data encoding
angles.query: Cleveland McGill graphical perception ranking position length angle area color accuracy study, perceptually uniform OKLCH sequential and diverging colormap construction, ColorBrewer Viridis colorblind-safe palette research
angles.rationale: Area 1's measured core: which encodings are accurate and why, and how to build color scales that survive CVD and non-color-encoding requirements. Targets peer-reviewed HCI/vis (Cleveland & McGill 1984, Harrower & Brewer, IEEE VIS colormap work) so every claimed perceptual ranking or threshold has a citable origin rather than folklore.

angles.label: authoritative component-pattern and accessibility canon
angles.query: Nielsen Norman Group and W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices guidance on modal dialog vs inline expansion vs routed page, drawer bottom sheet focus trap inert focus restore, progressive disclosure accordion details summary, card UI failure modes and alternatives to card grids
angles.rationale: Area 2 plus the non-negotiable accessibility constraint. NN/g supplies documented failure modes (card-grid sameness, truncation, weak information scent), APG supplies exact keyboard/focus/inert semantics for drawers, sheets and modals, and Apple HIG / Material supply platform sheet conventions — all primary sources rather than listicles.

angles.label: emerging 2025-2026 style movements and the anti-generic discourse
angles.query: named web design aesthetic movements 2026 beyond brutalism and glassmorphism — anti-design, spatial and Liquid Glass, editorial revival, dimensional type — and critique of the AI-default templated homogenized website look
angles.rationale: Area 3, and the pipeline's anti-template core rule. Needs current practitioner writing (Codrops, Awwwards, Rauno Freiberg, Emil Kowalski, design-press critique) to name both what is newly legible as a movement with its own failure mode, and what has calcified into the Tailwind/AI-default cliché the pipeline must explicitly avoid.

angles.label: web-native motion implementation: transitions, scrollytelling, timing numbers
angles.query: MDN View Transitions API and CSS scroll-driven animations for shared element container transform, SVG chart entrance and morphing animation, NYT Pudding Reuters scrollytelling scroll-linked chart transitions, spring physics vs duration easing and Material Design motion duration guidance with prefers-reduced-motion alternatives
angles.rationale: Areas 4 and 5 together, filtered through the implementability constraint. MDN/W3C establish what is CSS-native and cheap versus runtime-heavy, newsroom graphics desks supply scroll-linked chart choreography, and Material/Apple motion specs supply the duration and easing numbers that read as responsive versus sluggish — with reduced-motion handling in the same query so each technique arrives with its designed still.

angles.label: evidence base for loading, progress and perceived performance
angles.query: research evidence skeleton screens vs spinners vs progress bars perceived duration, Nielsen 0.1 1 10 second response time limits Miller 1968 Card 1991, progressive streaming rendering, optimistic UI, Core Web Vitals LCP and CLS layout shift avoidance
angles.rationale: Area 6, explicitly hunting numbers and their provenance. The skeleton-screen advantage is widely repeated but thinly measured, so this angle must separate actual studies (Miller, Card, Nielsen's response-time limits, the few controlled skeleton experiments) from folklore, and tie back to the pipeline's sub-100KB shell and 1.5s LCP budget via Core Web Vitals primary documentation.

results.title: View Transition API — MDN Web Docs
results.snippet: Primary spec-level reference for shared-element/container-transform motion, covering both same-document (`document.startViewTransition()`) and cross-document MPA transitions via `@view-transition { navigation: auto }`. Supplies the exact pseudo-element tree the pipeline would style (`::view-transition-old/new/group/image-pair`), `view-transition-name` for element pairing, and the default 250ms cross-fade. Critical for the implementability constraint: cross-document transitions are CSS-only and cost zero JS bytes, so they belong in the <100KB shell tier rather than the deferred heavy layer. MDN also documents that reduced-motion is NOT automatic — the designed still must be authored explicitly inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` overriding the `::view-transition-*` animations.

results.title: Scroll-driven animation timelines — CSS — MDN Web Docs
results.snippet: The authoritative account of `animation-timeline`, `scroll()` and `view()` timelines, `scroll-timeline-name`/`view-timeline`, and `animation-range` — i.e. scroll-linked reveals and chart entrance choreography with no scroll listener, no IntersectionObserver, no rAF loop, and no library. This is the CSS-native/cheap versus runtime-heavy dividing line the pipeline needs: `view()` timelines cover the common 'element enters viewport, animate it' case that most sites still ship GSAP/ScrollTrigger for, and they run off the main thread on the compositor. Also the correct place to note the failure mode — scroll-coupled motion cannot be paused by the user, so large translations/rotations on `scroll(root)` need a reduced-motion gate that swaps to a static composed state rather than `animation: none`.

results.title: Easing and duration — Material Design 3 (tokens and specs)
results.snippet: The attributable source for the duration numbers the survey asks for: the full `md.sys.motion.duration.short1–4 / medium1–4 / long1–4 / extra-long1–4` ladder (50ms up to 1000ms) and the named easing curves as literal cubic-bezier values — Emphasized (0.2, 0, 0, 1) and its decelerate/accelerate split for entering versus exiting, Standard, and Legacy. Gives the platform-guidance rules of thumb the pipeline can cite instead of folklore: small utility transitions and icon/ripple feedback at the short tokens, container transforms and page-level transitions on emphasized easing at the medium/long tokens, larger screens getting longer durations and small screens/wearables shorter. Directly usable as CSS custom properties, so it is a token table for CRAFT.md rather than a runtime dependency.

results.title: Executing UX Animations: Duration and Motion Characteristics — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: NN/G's practitioner-research guidance on how long a UI animation should last and what motion characteristics read as responsive versus sluggish — the usability-side counterpart to Material's token table, and the source to cite for the 'under ~100ms feels instant, roughly 100–500ms is the usable band for UI transitions, beyond ~1s reads as sluggish/blocking' claims that otherwise circulate as folklore. Covers easing choice by intent (entering versus exiting versus persistent elements), distance-scaled duration, and the argument that animation must carry meaning (spatial continuity, state change, attention direction) rather than decoration — which maps onto the disclosure/drawer/list/chart motion questions in Area 4 and the micro-interaction feedback questions in Area 5.

results.title: Response Time Limits: 0.1s, 1s, 10s — Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: The original, properly attributable source for the three response-time thresholds (0.1s = feels instantaneous, direct manipulation, no feedback needed; 1.0s = flow of thought preserved but delay noticed; 10s = limit of attention, needs a determinate progress indicator). Nielsen grounds these in Miller (1968) and Card et al. (1991) human-factors work and notes they are properties of human perception, not hardware, so they have not moved since 1993. This is the evidence base underneath both the micro-interaction timing budgets (Area 5) and the skeleton-versus-spinner-versus-progress-bar decision (Area 6): below 1s show nothing, 1–10s show an indeterminate/skeleton state, above 10s show determinate progress plus a time estimate.

results.title: Scrolling into the Newsroom: A vocabulary for scrollytelling techniques in visual online articles — Information Design Journal
results.snippet: Peer-reviewed (Information Design Journal) taxonomy derived from an analysis of real newsroom output, and exactly the kind of source the brief prefers over listicles. It names five reusable scrollytelling techniques with their mechanics — graphic sequence (text blocks pass over a pinned graphic that is swapped wholesale per block), animated transition (a pinned graphic interpolates between states, showing intermediate frames, i.e. scroll-linked chart morphing), panning and zooming, scrolling through movies, and show/auto-play of animated content. The distinction between 'sequence' (discrete swap, cheap, degrades to a stack of static figures) and 'animated transition' (continuous interpolation, expensive, needs a designed reduced-motion still) is precisely the mechanics/fails/right-when split STYLES.md entries require, and it gives named patterns for scroll-linked chart choreography that can be cited rather than invented.

results.title: Dialog (Modal) Pattern — ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (W3C/WAI)
results.snippet: The primary normative-adjacent source for Area 2's non-negotiable accessibility constraint on drawers, sheets and modals. Specifies exactly what the pipeline must ship: role="dialog" + aria-modal="true", accessible name via aria-labelledby/aria-label, focus moved into the dialog on open (generally the first focusable element, or a specific element via autofocus), tab sequence contained so Tab/Shift+Tab cycle within the dialog and never escape it, Escape closes, and focus RESTORED to the invoking element on close. Also states that aria-modal (ARIA 1.1) replaces per-element aria-hidden for marking background content inert — the modern implementation being the `inert` attribute. Gives the same contract for non-modal dialogs, which is the correct base for side panels/drawers that should not trap focus. Directly usable as the acceptance checklist for any drawer/sheet/modal CRAFT.md entry.

results.title: Cards: UI-Component Definition — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: NN/g's definitional article on cards, and the authoritative statement of the card's intended job and its documented failure modes. Defines a card as a high-information-scent container meant to entice a click through to a separate detail page — which makes weak information scent the diagnostic failure, not a matter of taste. Names when cards are the WRONG container: dense comparable data belongs in a table, linear flows (forms, sequences) belong in continuous layout. Companion NN/g eye-tracking work on irregular card layouts found users scan in semi-random back-and-forth patterns, wasting time and mental energy — the primary evidence against masonry/ragged card grids. Also the source of the truncation critique (excerpts must be authored for the card, not machine-truncated mid-thought). This is the citation that lets the repo write the card's "Fails" clause from research rather than opinion.

results.title: Bottom Sheets: Definition and UX Guidelines — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: NN/g's dedicated treatment of the bottom-sheet/drawer family: what distinguishes modal from non-modal (persistent) sheets, detent/partial-height behavior, drag handles as the affordance that signals resizability, and when a sheet beats a full-screen change of context. Pairs with NN/g's "Accidental Dismissal of Overlays" finding that swipe/tap-outside dismissal silently destroys work on mobile — the sheet's characteristic failure mode, and the reason a sheet needs a visible, keyboard-reachable close control rather than gesture-only dismissal. Supplies the platform-neutral half of the sheet vocabulary the repo currently lacks; combine with the APG dialog pattern for the focus contract.

results.title: Accordions on Desktop: When and How to Use — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: Covers progressive disclosure as an actual decision rule rather than a slogan, and is the source for the modal-vs-inline-expansion-vs-page arbitration the survey needs. Positions accordions as progressive disclosure where the heading carries the summary and the panel the supplementary detail; recommends them for content-heavy pages where users will NOT need several panels at once (the failure mode being users forced to open many, which is worse than a plain long page). Crucially, NN/g's overlay guidance says to avoid overlays where possible and use an accordion or a full page instead, and reserve overlays for small non-scrolling content — a direct, citable ranking of inline expansion above modals. Maps cleanly onto the native, zero-JS `<details>/<summary>` implementation, so it is cheap against the sub-100KB shell budget.

results.title: <dialog> element — MDN Web Docs
results.snippet: The web-native, budget-friendly implementation path for everything the APG dialog pattern requires, and the answer to "CSS/HTML-native (cheap) vs heavy runtime". showModal() promotes the dialog to the top layer, renders a ::backdrop pseudo-element (styleable, so the scrim can be designed rather than a generic black 50%), makes all other document content implicitly inert — removed from tab order AND the accessibility tree — sets aria-modal="true" implicitly, moves focus to the first focusable element (or `autofocus`), traps tab, handles Escape natively, and restores focus to the invoker on close. That is a full focus-trap/restore/inert stack for roughly zero JS bytes, replacing the usual focus-trap library. Note the caveat it documents: modal dialogs escape ancestor inertness, and initial focus placement should be declared explicitly with autofocus rather than left to the default.

results.title: Sheets — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: The platform-convention source for the sheet family the angle calls for: a sheet is for a scoped task closely related to the current context, versus a full-screen modal for a self-contained task that warrants taking over. Documents detents (partial-height resizable sheets, iOS 16+), how to keep swipe-to-dismiss coherent when a navigation stack lives inside a sheet, and — relevant to the modal-vs-inline decision — Apple's preference for a NONMODAL view when showing extra options or tools without interrupting the main task. Flag for the repo: these are native-platform conventions, so a web portfolio borrows the mental model (detents, scoped task, drag-to-dismiss) but must re-supply keyboard operability, focus restore and inert background itself, since none of it comes free off-platform.

results.title: Cleveland & McGill (1984), "Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods", JASA 79(387):531-554
results.snippet: THE primary source for the perceptual ranking the pipeline needs to cite instead of folklore. Full text PDF of the JASA paper that defines the elementary perceptual tasks and orders them by measured decoding accuracy: (1) position along a common scale, (2) position along non-aligned scales, (3) length / direction / angle, (4) area, (5) volume / curvature, (6) shading and colour saturation. Also the origin of the bar-vs-pie result (position/length beat angle) and of the dot-plot-over-pie recommendation. Any STYLES.md or CRAFT.md line claiming 'position is the most accurate encoding' should attribute here, with the caveat that the ranking is task-specific (proportion judgement of two values), not a universal law — it does not cover pattern-finding, trend, or overview tasks.

results.title: Heer & Bostock (2010), "Crowdsourcing Graphical Perception: Using Mechanical Turk to Assess Visualization Design", ACM CHI
results.snippet: The modern replication that makes the 1984 ranking citable with numbers rather than as received wisdom. Reproduces Cleveland & McGill's proportional-judgement experiment on a crowdsourced pool and extends it to encodings the original never tested — circular area (bubble charts) and rectangular area (treemaps) — confirming position < length < angle < area in log-absolute-error, and separately measuring luminance-contrast and rectangular-area (Stevens exponent) effects. Directly relevant to Area 1: gives a defensible basis for 'do not encode a quantity you want compared as bubble size', and its spatial-encoding/luminance experiments feed the non-color-encoding requirement. Web-native context too — Bostock is D3's author, so the tested stimuli are SVG-renderable.

results.title: Harrower & Brewer (2003), "ColorBrewer.org: An Online Tool for Selecting Colour Schemes for Maps", The Cartographic Journal 40(1):27-37 (refereed paper, full PDF)
results.snippet: The refereed origin of the sequential / diverging / qualitative taxonomy the pipeline is missing, and of scheme-per-class-count design. Explicitly ties scheme choice to (a) number of data classes, (b) measurement level of the data, and (c) the end-use environment — CRT, LCD, print, projection, photocopy — plus colourblind-safe and grayscale-safe flags per scheme. Directly usable: the palettes are small, fixed hex lists that can be vendored as CSS custom properties with zero byte cost and no CDN, satisfying the self-hosted constraint. Caveat to flag: ColorBrewer schemes are hand-tuned in Munsell/CIELAB-adjacent reasoning, not algorithmically perceptually uniform, and top out around 9-12 classes — for continuous ramps prefer a constructed uniform map.

results.title: Crameri, Shephard & Heron (2020), "The misuse of colour in science communication", Nature Communications 11:5444
results.snippet: Peer-reviewed evidence for the two failure modes a portfolio pipeline must avoid by rule: colour maps with uneven perceptual gradients (rainbow/jet) that manufacture false boundaries and hide real ones, and red-green pairings unreadable under colour-vision deficiency. Provides the 'Scientific colour maps' family (batlow, vik, roma, etc.), each perceptually uniform, readable in CVD simulation, and readable in grayscale — the grayscale property is the practical proof of a non-color redundant encoding. Includes a short, quotable guide plus CVD- and grayscale-simulation as a checkable acceptance test, which maps cleanly onto the pipeline's 'evidence and provenance' and 'non-color encoding' constraints.

results.title: Nuñez, Anderton & Renslow (2018), "Optimizing colormaps with consideration for color vision deficiency to enable accurate interpretation of scientific data", PLOS ONE 13(7):e0199239
results.snippet: Shows the *construction method*, not just a palette list: the authors state the optimisation objective (monotonic, near-linear lightness ramp in CAM02-UCS; minimal perceptual distortion under deuteranomaly simulation) and derive cividis from viridis by it. This is the citable answer to 'how do you build a sequential scale rather than pick one', and it documents the honest trade — viridis is colourblind-*friendly* but still uses a blue-to-yellow-green path that shifts under CVD, while cividis is optimised so a CVD and non-CVD viewer read near-identical structure. Useful for the pipeline because the same objective (monotone L*, controlled C and H) is directly expressible in OKLCH in CSS, so bespoke per-run scales can be generated instead of reusing a recognisable stock ramp — supporting the anti-template rule.

results.title: W3C, CSS Color Module Level 4 — oklab()/oklch(), color interpolation and gradient interpolation spaces
results.snippet: The normative, web-native bridge from the perceptual-colour literature to shippable CSS. Defines oklab()/oklch() (Ottosson's Oklab, fitted to perceptual data so Euclidean distance approximates perceived difference and hue stays stable across chroma), and specifies interpolation behaviour for gradients and color-mix(), including hue-interpolation methods for the cylindrical form. Practical consequences for the pipeline: perceptually uniform sequential and diverging ramps become a few CSS declarations (near-zero bytes, no runtime, no chart library, degrades via @supports to sRGB stops); a diverging scale is built as two monotone-L* arms meeting at a neutral; and holding L* monotone gives the grayscale/CVD-redundant reading Crameri's test demands. Flag as CSS-native/cheap tier, and note gamut-clipping needs checking against display-p3 vs sRGB.

results.title: Response Time Limits: 0.1s / 1s / 10s — Jakob Nielsen (NN/g, 1993)
results.snippet: THE provenance source for the three numbers everyone quotes. Nielsen states plainly that "the basic advice regarding response times has been about the same for thirty years [Miller 1968; Card et al. 1991]" — i.e. 0.1s = feels instantaneous (no feedback needed beyond the result), 1.0s = flow of thought stays uninterrupted (delay noticed, no special feedback), 10s = limit of attention on the dialogue (beyond it, give a percent-done indicator and let the user do something else). Citable primaries: Miller, R.B. (1968) "Response time in man-computer conversational transactions"; Card, Robertson & Mackinlay (1991) "The information visualizer: an information workspace", CHI'91, 181–188. Critically for the report's folklore/measured split: these are perceptual-psychology thresholds from mainframe-era HCI, NOT web-loading measurements — cite them for interaction latency (hover, press, disclosure, chart transitions) and flag that extending them to page loads is extrapolation. Directly sets the ceiling for micro-interaction timings in Area 5 and the "when does a loading affordance need to exist at all" question in Area 6.

results.title: How the Core Web Vitals metrics thresholds were defined — web.dev (Chrome team)
results.snippet: Primary documentation of WHY the CWV numbers are what they are, which is exactly the provenance the angle demands. Explains the threshold methodology (quality-of-experience research, achievability across the HTTP Archive corpus, 75th-percentile measurement segmented mobile/desktop) and gives the CLS derivation directly: internal testing found shifts of 0.15 and above were "consistently perceived as disruptive" while 0.1 and below were "noticeable but not excessively disruptive." Anchors LCP ≤ 2.5s and CLS ≤ 0.1 as measured-and-justified rather than folklore. Note the tension to flag for the pipeline: the repo budget of LCP < 1.5s is STRICTER than the documented good threshold — that is a self-imposed target, not a standards number, and should be labelled as such. Companion primaries for the same numbers: web.dev/articles/lcp, web.dev/articles/cls, web.dev/articles/optimize-cls (layout-shift avoidance: dimension attributes on media, reserved space for injected content, font-swap strategy).

results.title: A Bone to Pick with Skeleton Screens — Viget (controlled study, n=136)
results.snippet: The strongest published counter-evidence to the "skeletons feel faster" consensus, and the single most useful citation for separating measured results from repetition. In a randomised test of skeleton vs. spinner vs. blank screen with 136 participants, the skeleton screen performed WORST on every metric measured: users took longer to complete the task, were more likely to rate the wait negatively, and estimated the wait as longer than the spinner or blank-screen groups. Because it contradicts the received wisdom (and Chung's and Mejtoft's results), it establishes that the skeleton advantage is condition-dependent, not a law — the correct framing for a STYLES/CRAFT entry is a documented failure mode ("skeleton whose geometry does not match the final layout, or which persists past ~1s, reads as a stall and inflates perceived duration"), not a blanket recommendation. Also flags the byte/complexity argument: a skeleton that mispredicts final layout causes the very CLS it was supposed to prevent.

results.title: The effect of skeleton screens: users' perception of speed and ease of navigation — Mejtoft et al., ECCE '18 (ACM)
results.snippet: The peer-reviewed counterweight to Viget, and the only proper conference-published skeleton experiment in this area (Proceedings of the 36th European Conference on Cognitive Ergonomics, ACM DL). Found the skeleton-screen page scored higher on average for both perceived speed and perceived ease of navigation — but with the honest wrinkle that spinner-group participants were actually FASTER at locating the target article on first visit. Pair with Viget and with Bill Chung's independently-run mobile test (n=80, randomised paradigm order AND randomised durations, skeleton best on perceived duration and on self-reported emotional response, blank screen worst) to show the state of the evidence is: three small studies, conflicting directions, no meta-analysis, effect sizes modest. That is the accurate provenance verdict for the report — "weakly and inconsistently supported", not "proven". Chung's secondary finding is the actionable craft detail: slow, steady skeleton motion is perceived as shorter than fast or rapid motion (small n — flag as suggestive).

results.title: Progress Indicators Make a Slow System Less Insufferable — NN/g
results.snippet: Authoritative source for the indicator-selection rule keyed to duration, and for the three classic benefits (reassures the system has not crashed; sets expectation of how long, freeing the user to do something else; gives something to look at, making the wait less painful — these trace back to Myers 1985 via Nielsen's Usability Engineering). The operative numbered guidance: use a percent-done indicator for processes of 10 seconds or more, because it is the most informative wait feedback — it conveys progress made, work remaining, and approximate duration; below that, a looping/indeterminate animation suffices; below ~1s, show nothing (a flashed spinner is worse than no spinner). NN/g also reports users express higher satisfaction and tolerate longer waits with a dynamic indicator. Companion NN/g pages worth citing alongside: "Visibility of System Status" (Heuristic #1), "Designing for Long Waits and Interruptions", and the NN/g video "Skeleton Screens vs. Progress Bars vs. Spinners".

results.title: Effective Skeleton Screens — Tim Kadlec
results.snippet: A named web-performance practitioner explicitly reconciling the contradictory skeleton evidence (Viget vs. Chung/Mejtoft) into implementable conditions, which is what turns the studies into a CRAFT.md row. Argues the wins and losses are explained by execution, not by the pattern: the skeleton must closely mirror the geometry of the content that replaces it (otherwise you get a jarring swap and real CLS), must not over-promise more content than arrives, and must be reserved for waits long enough to warrant it — otherwise it advertises slowness. Web-native and cheap in the pipeline's terms: a skeleton is pure CSS/HTML boxes, inlinable in the sub-100KB shell with effectively zero JS, degrades to a designed static still under prefers-reduced-motion (grey blocks with no shimmer, satisfying the "never animation: none" rule), and needs no canvas/WebGL fallback at all. Pairs naturally with streaming/progressive HTML rendering as the alternative that removes the need for a placeholder entirely — see eBay's "Async Fragments: Rediscovering Progressive HTML Rendering with Marko" (innovation.ebayinc.com) for the out-of-order early-flush technique and its measured effect on real and perceived load time.

results.title: The generic style of AI web design — Kyle Chayka Industries
results.snippet: The single strongest primary source for the pipeline's anti-template core rule. Chayka (author of Filterworld, on cultural homogenization / 'AirSpace') names the AI-default web look as a legible style in its own right: LLM coding tools ship baked-in defaults, and absent active pushback the user receives 'the lowest common acceptable denominator of aesthetics and taste.' Names Claude Design specifically. This is design-press critique by a named critic rather than an agency listicle, and it supplies the framing sentence for a 'what to avoid' section: the generic look is not an absence of style, it is a style with a name and a source. Supports the anti-template rule directly; no conflict with any budget or a11y constraint.

results.title: Web Design Trends 2026: What Actually Held Up After Six Months — Studio Meyer
results.snippet: Rare trend piece structured almost exactly like the repo's four-part STYLES.md shape: each named movement gets a shipping verdict and a failure mode. Separates what actually ships (bento grid — now so default across major tech companies that it IS the cliché; dark-mode-primary; token-based systems; anti-grid brutalism as deliberate counter-positioning) from demo-only looks (kinetic typography 'almost never ships in production' because it 'fights screen readers, fights search crawlers'; organic blob shapes 'almost never ship on conversion-critical flows'; WebGL restricted to 'when the brand IS the experience'). Gives a measured-ish cost number for Glassmorphism 2.0 (15-30% FPS drop on mid-tier Android) — flag as vendor-measured, not peer-reviewed. Money quote for the anti-template rule: 'when everyone else looks like Apple, looking different becomes the differentiator.' Directly usable as new STYLES.md 'Fails' clauses and as a cliché blocklist (bento grid, blobs, kinetic type).

results.title: 2025: A Very Special Year in Review — Codrops
results.snippet: The named practitioner-source the angle brief asked for, and the best inventory of what the creative-dev community actually built in 2025 across 51 published tutorials. Concrete technique names to cross-check against the existing 72: WebGPU and TSL (Three.js Shading Language), dithering shaders as a retro-aesthetic technique, procedural generation, particle systems, infinite/3D/wavy carousels, draggable interactive grids, scroll-smoother and parallax, Rive vector animation with data binding, GSAP going fully free in 2025 (with SplitText and MorphSVG now unpaywalled — a real change to what a self-hosted, vendored pipeline can legally ship). Caveat for the deliverable: Codrops indexes demos, not production sites, so pair every entry here with the Studio Meyer shipping verdict before promoting it to a style; most of these violate the sub-100KB shell and belong strictly in the deferred heavy layer.

results.title: Meet Liquid Glass — WWDC25, Apple Developer
results.snippet: Primary source (platform HIG-tier, not commentary) for the single biggest named movement of 2025-2026 that the existing 32-style list does not cover. Defines Liquid Glass as an adaptive physics-based *material* rather than a decoration — mechanics are lensing/refraction of what is behind the surface, specular highlight response to motion, and adaptive tinting to hold contrast over unpredictable backdrops. Important distinction for a STYLES.md entry: this is the successor to, and explicitly not, the flat blur-and-transparency glassmorphism the pipeline may already document. 'Right when' condition per Apple: a floating control layer above content, never the content layer itself.

results.title: Getting Clarity on Apple's Liquid Glass — CSS-Tricks
results.snippet: The web-implementability half of the Liquid Glass entry, and the reason it survives the pipeline's constraints. Works through what CSS can and cannot natively do here — backdrop-filter gets the blur but not the refraction/lensing, which needs SVG filters (feDisplacementMap/feTurbulence) or a shader, i.e. a real fork between a cheap CSS/SVG-native tier and a heavy runtime tier. Pair with the documented failure mode from the same news cycle: Apple shipped a Reduce Transparency escape hatch and then a 'Tinted' setting in iOS 26.1 after legibility backlash — semi-transparent overlays go illegible over busy or low-light backdrops. That is a WCAG-contrast violation waiting to happen, so any Liquid Glass style entry must ship the tinted/opaque variant as its designed reduced state, not as an afterthought.

results.title: Craft — Rauno Freiberg
results.snippet: The named practitioner reference from the brief (Freiberg, design engineer at Vercel, author of cmdk). A running collection of short notes on the small decisions that make an interface feel deliberate rather than assembled — the companion essay 'Invisible Details of Interaction Design' (rauno.me/craft/interaction-design) is the canonical practitioner text on why some interactions feel right. Relevance is medium for Area 3 specifically (it names no aesthetic movement) but high for the pipeline's underlying thesis and for Areas 4-5: it argues distinctiveness comes from accumulated micro-decisions, not from picking a different style label — which is the strongest available counter-argument to a style-catalogue approach and worth quoting as a caveat in the report. Companion source in the same circle: Emil Kowalski's interfacecraft.dev (40+ articles, Linear design engineer).

claims.claim: The View Transition API is a single native mechanism covering both same-document (SPA) DOM-state transitions via Document.startViewTransition() and cross-document (MPA) navigation transitions via the @view-transition CSS at-rule — meaning shared-element/page-to-page transitions are web-platform-native and do not require a client-side router or animation runtime.
claims.quote: The View Transition API provides a mechanism for easily creating animated transitions between different website and element views. This includes animating between DOM states in a single-page app (SPA), and animating the navigation between documents in a multi-page app (MPA).

claims.claim: Transitions are driven entirely through a CSS pseudo-element tree (::view-transition → ::view-transition-group() → ::view-transition-image-pair() → ::view-transition-old()/::view-transition-new()), where the old view is a static snapshot and the new view is a live representation — so the animation is authored in plain CSS keyframes with zero JS animation library bytes.
claims.quote: ::view-transition-old() — A static snapshot of the old view, before the transition. ::view-transition-new() — A live representation of the new view, after the transition.

claims.claim: The view-transition-name CSS property is the mechanism for shared-element / container-transform motion: naming an element opts it into its own snapshot so it animates independently of the rest of the page, and view-transition-class / view-transition-scope extend and isolate that behaviour.
claims.quote: Specifies the view transition snapshot that selected elements will participate in, which enables an element to be animated separately from the rest of the page during a view transition.

claims.claim: <link rel="expect"> blocks document rendering until designated critical content has been parsed, which MDN presents as the way to guarantee a consistent first paint (and therefore a consistent cross-document view transition) across supporting browsers — a render-blocking trade-off directly relevant to LCP budgets and layout-shift avoidance.
claims.quote: Identifies the most critical content in the associated document for the user's initial view of the page. Document rendering will be blocked until the critical content has been parsed, ensuring a consistent first paint — and therefore, view transition — across all supporting browsers.

claims.claim: MDN attributes concrete accessibility failure modes — loss of reading position, focus confusion, and anomalous live-region announcements — to having old and new content simultaneously present in the DOM, the condition the API's snapshot model is designed to avoid; the reference page itself documents no automatic prefers-reduced-motion handling, so a designed reduced-motion variant must be authored by hand.
claims.quote: Accessibility issues like loss of reading position, focus confusion, and strange live region announcement behavior can also result from having the new and old content both present in the DOM at once.

claims.claim: CSS scroll-driven animations link keyframe progress to scroll position without any JavaScript scroll listener or IntersectionObserver, and run off the main thread — making scroll-linked reveals and scrollytelling chart transitions a zero-JS, zero-byte-runtime technique that fits inside a <100KB shell (satisfies the web-native / cheap-vs-heavy-runtime constraint).
claims.quote: JavaScript scroll-driven animations require `scroll` event listeners and `IntersectionObserver` on main thread ... CSS scroll-driven animations are performant and don't block the main thread

claims.claim: There are exactly two timeline types with different semantics: a scroll progress timeline maps a scroller's scroll offset to 0%–100%, while a view progress timeline maps a subject element's visibility within the scrollport — 0% when it starts intersecting the end edge, 100% when it exits the start edge. Because 100% is reached only as the element leaves the viewport, entrance animations must finish well before 100% (e.g. keyframes at 20%/50%/80%), otherwise the reveal completes off-screen.
claims.quote: 100% reached as element leaves viewport, so complete effects before 100% (use 20%, 50%, 80% keyframes)

claims.claim: MDN's documented reduced-motion pattern for scroll-driven animation is `animation-timeline: none` inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`, which disassociates the element from all timelines and prevents the animation entirely — this is an off-switch, so it directly conflicts with a pipeline rule requiring a DESIGNED reduced-motion still rather than simply disabling motion; the designed still must be authored separately as the element's static state.
claims.quote: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .optionalAnimations { animation-timeline: none; } } ... Setting `animation-timeline: none` disassociates element from all timelines, preventing animation.

claims.claim: The `animation` shorthand resets `animation-timeline` to `auto`, so `animation-timeline` must be declared after the shorthand (and with sufficient specificity) or the scroll-driven binding is silently lost and the animation falls back to the document time timeline.
claims.quote: The `animation` shorthand resets `animation-timeline` to `auto`

claims.claim: `animation-duration` has no effect on a scroll-driven animation's actual duration; the documented convention is `animation-duration: 1ms`, both because Firefox requires a non-zero duration and because it makes the animation effectively invisible in browsers that do not support scroll-driven timelines — giving a built-in no-support fallback path.
claims.quote: For scroll-driven animations, `animation-duration` **does not affect** animation duration ... Ensures Firefox compatibility (requires non-zero duration) ... Hides animation effect in unsupported browsers

claims.claim: 0.1 second is the threshold below which a UI response reads as instantaneous, and no feedback indicator is needed at all — this sets the ceiling for micro-interaction feedback latency (hover, press, focus, toggle) in the pipeline's micro-interaction and motion vocabulary.
claims.quote: 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously, meaning that no special feedback is necessary except to display the result.

claims.claim: 1.0 second is the limit for keeping a user's flow of thought uninterrupted; the delay is noticed but tolerated, and between 0.1s and 1.0s no special feedback (spinner, skeleton) is warranted — meaning skeleton screens and spinners deployed under 1s are unjustified by this guidance.
claims.quote: Normally, no special feedback is necessary during delays of more than 0.1 but less than 1.0 second

claims.claim: 10 seconds is the limit for holding attention on a single dialogue; beyond it users task-switch and must reorient on return, which is the documented basis for percent-done progress indicators (as opposed to indeterminate spinners) on long operations.
claims.quote: 10 seconds is about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue.

claims.claim: Beyond 10 seconds users leave the task, so the design deliverable is not just a progress indicator but a reorientation state on return — relevant to designing loading/empty/error states as first-class deliverables.
claims.quote: Assume that users will need to reorient themselves when they return to the UI after a delay of more than 10 seconds.

claims.claim: These thresholds are measured human-perception findings from HCI literature (Miller 1968; Card, Robertson & Mackinlay 1991; Myers 1985 on percent-done indicators), not folklore or platform convention, and have been stable across decades of hardware change — so they can be cited as measured rather than asserted.
claims.quote: The basic advice regarding response times has been about the same for thirty years [Miller 1968; Card et al. 1991]

result.publishDate: 1993-01-01 (excerpt from Nielsen, Usability Engineering, Ch. 5; NNG republication updated later — article text references the guidelines holding "for 46 years now", implying a revision circa 2014)

claims.claim: NN/g's baseline duration range for UI animation is 100–500 ms, scaled to complexity and travel distance, with 500 ms as the point where animation starts to feel obstructive; the practical working band is 100–400 ms, and 400 ms is reserved for large movements on large screens. These are stated as craft heuristics in the article, not as results of a measured experiment — the only number with a research lineage is the ~100 ms perceptibility/immediacy floor, which links out to Nielsen's response-time limits.
claims.quote: In general, the duration of most animations should be in the range of 100–500 ms, depending on complexity and on how far the element is traveling. … At 500ms, animations start to feel like a real drag for users — they become cumbersome and annoying. … In most cases, a range of 100–400 ms is appropriate, with 400ms being a very slow animation, to be used only for big movements across large screens.

claims.claim: Duration should be tiered by the size of the state change: micro-interaction feedback (checkbox, toggle) at roughly 100 ms, and substantial screen changes such as a modal entering the viewport at 200–300 ms. This gives a directly usable two-tier number set for micro-interaction versus drawer/sheet/modal motion.
claims.quote: Simple feedback animations, such as showing a checkbox or toggle switch, should be roughly 100 ms (0.10 seconds) in total duration. … When animation involves substantial screen changes, such as when a modal window moves into view, a duration of 200–300 ms can be appropriate.

claims.claim: Exit animations should be shorter than entrance animations for the same element — a popup taking 300 ms to appear should take only 200–250 ms to dismiss. This asymmetry is a concrete, checkable rule for drawer/sheet/modal open-versus-close timing.
claims.quote: a popup window may take 300ms to appear, but only 200 or 250ms to disappear

claims.claim: Linear timing functions are wrong for UI motion; ease-out (fast start, decelerating finish) is the default recommendation for most UI animation. This is a CSS-native, zero-byte technique (`transition-timing-function`) — no runtime required — and directly contradicts a `linear` default.
claims.quote: Completely linear motion looks weird and unnatural to users. … Most frequently, you'll want to use an ease-out animation, that starts quickly but slows down.

claims.claim: NN/g's stated reduced-motion remedy is to REMOVE animation for users who set the reduce-motion preference, and it names parallax, carousel auto-advance and scroll-jacking as triggers for dizziness, nausea and migraine in users with vestibular disorders. This CONFLICTS with the pipeline's rule that every technique must ship a designed reduced-motion still rather than `animation: none` — NN/g is the authoritative source behind the removal convention the pipeline is deliberately overriding, so the repo rule needs to be stated as a deliberate, documented departure rather than an unexamined preference.
claims.quote: you should respect those users who have set their browser or device to 'reduce motion' by removing animations. … Parallax, carousel-forwarding animations, and scroll jacking can make users with vestibular disorders dizzy or nauseated and trigger migraines.

claims.claim: A modal dialog must implement a cyclic focus trap: Tab from the last tabbable element inside the dialog wraps to the first, Shift+Tab from the first wraps to the last, and neither key may move focus outside the dialog. This is the normative W3C/WAI keyboard contract any drawer, sheet, side panel or bottom sheet declared modal has to satisfy.
claims.quote: Moves focus to the next tabbable element inside the dialog. If focus is on the last tabbable element inside the dialog, moves focus to the first tabbable element inside the dialog. ... Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog

claims.claim: Marking a dialog as modal (aria-modal="true") is conditional on two simultaneous requirements — application code that prevents all users from interacting with outside content (inert background), and visual styling that obscures that outside content. A panel that only dims the background, or only sets aria-modal without inerting, violates the pattern.
claims.quote: only when both: (1) Application code prevents all users from interacting in any way with content outside of it. (2) Visual styling obscures the content outside of it.

claims.claim: On close, focus must be restored to the element that invoked the dialog, except where that element no longer exists or the workflow dictates another target. This makes focus restore a required deliverable of every modal/drawer implementation, not an optional polish step.
claims.quote: When a dialog closes, focus returns to the element that invoked the dialog

claims.claim: Escape must close the dialog, and the tab sequence should additionally contain a visible button-role element (close icon or cancel) that closes it — i.e. keyboard dismissal alone is insufficient, a visible dismissal affordance is strongly recommended.
claims.quote: It is strongly recommended that the tab sequence of all dialogs include a visible element with role `button` that closes the dialog, such as a close icon or cancel button.

claims.claim: Initial focus placement is context-dependent rather than a fixed "focus the first focusable element" rule: for irreversible actions focus the least destructive option, for large dialogs focus the title or first paragraph (via tabindex="-1") to avoid scroll jumps, and for informational dialogs focus the most frequently used control. This falsifies the common implementation shortcut of always autofocusing the first control.
claims.quote: For complex content with semantic structures: add `tabindex="-1"` to a static element at the start and focus it ... For irreversible actions: focus the least destructive option

result.publishDate: unknown — no publish or last-updated date exposed on the page (W3C/WAI ARIA Authoring Practices Guide is continuously maintained; current APG editions track ARIA 1.2/1.3)

claims.claim: NN/g defines a bottom sheet as a bottom-anchored overlay invoked by user interaction that uses progressive disclosure while keeping the underlying content visible — distinguishing it from a full-page overlay and giving the pipeline a precise definition for the drawers/sheets/side-panels vocabulary gap.
claims.quote: A bottom sheet is an overlay that is anchored to the bottom edge of a mobile device's screen and displays additional details or actions.

claims.claim: NN/g separates bottom sheets into three concrete variants with different modality contracts: modal (dark translucent scrim, background locked out), nonmodal (background remains interactive, sheet shown in parallel with main content), and expandable (starts nonmodal/minimized, swipe or tap promotes it to full-screen modal). This is a directly transferable component taxonomy for a STYLES/CRAFT-style pattern entry.
claims.quote: **Modal Bottom Sheets:** Force user interaction before accessing background content. A translucent dark scrim signals unavailability of locked-out content. **Nonmodal Bottom Sheets:** Allow continued interaction with background content while the sheet remains visible. ... **Expandable Sheets:** Start nonmodal in minimized state; users can swipe or tap to expand into full-screen modal format.

claims.claim: A grab handle alone is not an accessible dismissal affordance: NN/g prescribes a visible Close/X button in addition, because screen-reader users and users who cannot swipe precisely cannot rely on swipe-down, and vertical swipes are ambiguous with OS notification/control panels. This is a falsifiable accessibility requirement for any sheet the pipeline ships.
claims.quote: "Include a visible Close (or X) button" rather than relying exclusively on grab handles, improving accessibility for screen reader users and those unable to swipe precisely.

claims.claim: NN/g names three documented failure modes for sheets: stacking multiple sheets (confuses navigation hierarchy and dismissal), using sheets for page-to-page navigation flows, and using them for lengthy content or complex workflows — i.e. the correct alternatives for those cases are routed pages, not sheets. This supplies the 'Fails' half of a pattern entry and the modal-vs-inline-vs-routed-page decision rule.
claims.quote: **Use Only for Short Interactions:** "Bottom sheets should not be used for displaying lengthy content" or complex workflows requiring extended user engagement.

claims.claim: Sheets must honor the platform Back affordance for dismissal, not only gesture or button dismissal, to avoid disorientation — a concrete implementable requirement (history entry / popstate handling on web) beyond the usual focus-trap/Escape checklist.
claims.quote: **Support Back Button Dismissal:** Prevents disorientation and maintains normal navigation patterns.

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed empirical taxonomy of scrollytelling exists that reduces the technique space to exactly five named standard techniques — graphic sequences, animated transitions, panning and zooming, scrolling through movies, and showing/auto-playing animated content — derived from analysis of 50 published examples. This is a directly reusable, citable vocabulary for the pipeline's missing scroll-linked-chart-transition and data-storytelling material.
claims.quote: By analysing 50 examples, we have identified granular characteristics of scrollytelling elements, or 'scrollers', and grouped them into five standard techniques: graphic sequences, animated transitions, panning and zooming, scrolling through movies, and showing and auto-playing animated content.

claims.claim: The paper names 'scroller' as the atomic unit of scrollytelling analysis — a discrete scroll-linked element with enumerable granular characteristics — rather than treating scrollytelling as a whole-page property. This gives a component-level (not page-level) decomposition that maps onto a technique-table shape like CRAFT.md.
claims.quote: we have identified granular characteristics of scrollytelling elements, or 'scrollers', and grouped them into five standard techniques

claims.claim: As of the paper's 2022 publication, scrollytelling was documented in the peer-reviewed literature as expensive to produce, and the stated purpose of the vocabulary is to lower implementation cost — supporting the pipeline's two-tier budget concern that scroll-driven techniques are a deferred heavy layer, not shell-weight.
claims.quote: Despite its popularity, scrollytelling is still costly to produce. This study aims to generate a scrollytelling vocabulary for newsrooms and creative agencies... [to] implement scrollers faster and more easily.

claims.claim: The authors assert a documented gap in the research literature: prior to this 2022 study, few studies had systematically examined the variety of existing scrollytelling techniques. Any competing taxonomy of scrollytelling techniques predating it is therefore unlikely to be peer-reviewed, which constrains what can be cited as authoritative.
claims.quote: Despite its popularity, few studies have examined the variety of existing scrollytelling techniques.

claims.claim: The work is positioned by its own keywords inside the narrative-visualization and information-design research tradition rather than in web-development practice, meaning its technique names are medium-agnostic and carry no HTML/CSS/JS implementation guidance, byte cost, reduced-motion fallback, or accessibility specification — the pipeline must supply all three required states itself.
claims.quote: Keywords: data visualization, design research, infographics, information design, narrative visualization, online journalism, scrollytelling, visual storytelling

claims.claim: NN/G states accordions are the right pattern only when users need a few pieces of information from independent sections, and are wrong when the audience needs most or all of the content, because the required clicking fragments access to the page.
claims.quote: When users need most/all content, "excessive clicking interrupts people's interaction with the page."

claims.claim: The documented failure mode of accordions is compromised discoverability: content placed inside a collapsed panel can go entirely unseen if the heading does not entice expansion — so crucial information must never be hidden in a collapsed panel.
claims.quote: "Valuable content that is hidden under an accordion may be missed altogether" if headings fail to entice exploration.

claims.claim: Accessible accordion implementation requires that a collapsed panel's content be both visually hidden AND programmatically unreachable (i.e. removed from the accessibility tree / tab order, not merely clipped or made transparent).
claims.quote: "When the accordion is collapsed, ensure the content inside the panel is both visually hidden and programmatically unreachable."

claims.claim: NN/G recommends allowing multiple accordion sections to be open simultaneously (rather than auto-closing the previous one) and providing Expand All / Collapse All controls; auto-closing blocks cross-section comparison and the absence of Expand All forces manual expansion before printing.
claims.quote: "Allow users to open or collapse multiple sections at a time" ... Without "Expand All" buttons, "users are required to expand each accordion individually before printing."

claims.claim: Accordions are explicitly contraindicated for continuous narrative reading (news articles, stories), for deeply hierarchical content, and for pages with little content, where they produce an empty-looking page or cause users to lose their place.
claims.quote: Deep hierarchical content (users "may feel confused and lose track") ... Continuous reading experiences (news articles, narratives—"seamless reading experience" should be prioritized)

claims.claim: NN/g's operational definition of a card is a container for a few short related pieces of information that acts as a linked, high-information-scent summary of one conceptual unit, where clicking or tapping anywhere on the card goes to a details page — i.e. a card is a link surface, not a layout decoration. This gives the pipeline a falsifiable test for whether a component is legitimately a card.
claims.quote: A container for a few short, related pieces of information. It roughly resembles a playing card in size and shape, and is intended as a linked, short representation of a conceptual unit.

claims.claim: Cards are the wrong container for homogeneous collections: NN/g explicitly recommends a standard vertical list (or an image grid for narrowly-defined similar items) instead of cards when items are very homogeneous — which is exactly the case for a portfolio of similar project entries, making the default card grid a documented anti-pattern for that use.
claims.quote: When presenting very homogenous items (such as a list of similar blog posts, products, or news stories), consider using a standard vertical list of items (or, in certain cases where the items are similar and are all from a narrowly defined category, grids of images) instead of cards.

claims.claim: Card layouts have a documented failure mode for comparison tasks: because the flexible layout does not encode an order, eyetracking shows users scan in a semirandom pattern and re-visit the same items repeatedly, raising cognitive load relative to consistently-positioned list rows.
claims.quote: The flexible-card layout does not clearly indicate a hierarchy of stories in order, so the user looks around back and forth in a semirandom pattern

claims.claim: Cards suppress ranking and are measurably harder to scan than lists, so they are the wrong encoding for any ordered or search-like index; NN/g states both properties directly, which supports tables-as-index and editorial list indexes as the correct alternative when order or scanning matters.
claims.quote: Card layouts typically deemphasize the ranking of content

claims.claim: The mechanism that makes cards work is the Gestalt principle of common region — a visible boundary groups enclosed items more strongly than proximity does — meaning the grouping effect, not the shadow or the rounded corner, is the load-bearing part; a card's border/background can therefore be replaced by any common-region cue (rule, tint, whitespace field) without losing the grouping function.
claims.quote: Multiple items contained together within a boundary are more likely to be perceived as being grouped.

claims.claim: The native <dialog> element opened with showModal() provides browser-supplied modal semantics with no JS library: the rest of the page is rendered inert, Esc dismisses it (and with stacked dialogs, Esc closes only the last-shown one), and the element is implicitly exposed as aria-modal="true" — whereas show() or the open attribute yield a non-modal dialog exposed as aria-modal="false" that does NOT dismiss on Esc by default.
claims.quote: Modal dialog boxes block interaction with other UI elements, making the rest of the page inert, while non-modal dialog boxes allow interaction with the rest of the page. ... If multiple modal dialogs are open, pressing the Esc key should close only the last shown dialog. When using `<dialog>`, this behavior is provided by the browser. ... `<dialog>` elements invoked by the `showModal()` method implicitly have `aria-modal="true"`, whereas `<dialog>` elements invoked by the `show()` method or displayed using the `open` attribute or by changing the default `display` of a `<dialog>` are exposed as `[aria-modal="false"]`. ... A non-modal dialog does not dismiss via the Esc key by default

claims.claim: Initial focus for a modal dialog defaults to the first nested focusable element; MDN prescribes using the autofocus attribute to control it explicitly, recommends the <dialog> element itself as the focus target when the best placement is unknown (e.g. dynamically rendered content), and explicitly forbids putting tabindex on the <dialog>.
claims.quote: When using [`HTMLDialogElement.showModal()`] to open a `<dialog>`, focus is set on the first nested focusable element. ... Explicitly indicating the initial focus placement by using the [`autofocus`] attribute will help ensure initial focus is set on the element deemed the best initial focus placement for any particular dialog. ... the `<dialog>` element itself may provide the best initial focus placement. ... Do not add the `tabindex` property to the `<dialog>` element as it is not interactive and does not receive focus.

claims.claim: The `closedby` attribute declaratively controls which user-initiated dismissal mechanisms a dialog accepts — "any" (light dismiss by clicking outside, plus Esc, plus developer mechanism), "closerequest" (Esc plus developer mechanism), "none" (developer mechanism only) — and when absent or invalid the dialog defaults to "closerequest" if opened with showModal() and "none" otherwise.
claims.quote: if the `<dialog>` element does not have a valid `closedby` value specified, then if it was opened using [`showModal()`], it behaves as if the value was `"closerequest"` otherwise, it behaves as if the value was `"none"`.

claims.claim: Dialog open/close motion is achievable in pure CSS with no animation runtime, but requires three specific declarations because display is a discrete-animation property: a @starting-style rule for entry values, `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` on display and overlay, and `overlay` included in the transition list so top-layer removal is deferred until the transition finishes. Keyframe animations differ: no @starting-style and no overlay are needed, and display is set inside a keyframe instead.
claims.quote: Set `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` on the `display` and `overlay` transitions (or on the [`transition`] shorthand) to enable discrete transitions on these two properties that are not by default animatable. ... Include `overlay` in the transitions list to ensure the removal of the `<dialog>` from the top layer is deferred until the transition completes, again ensuring the transition is visible. ... When animating a `<dialog>` with CSS keyframe animations, there are some differences to note from transitions: You don't provide a `@starting-style`.

claims.claim: A <form method="dialog"> (or a submit button with formmethod="dialog") closes the dialog without submitting: form control state is saved but not sent, and the dialog's returnValue is set to the activated button's value — giving a zero-JS close-and-return-a-choice pattern. The <dialog> element itself has been Baseline/available across browsers since March 2022.
claims.quote: When a `<form>` within a `<dialog>` is submitted via the `dialog` method, the dialog box closes, the states of the form controls are saved but not submitted, and the [`returnValue`] property gets set to the value of the button that was activated. ... It's been available across browsers since March 2022.

claims.claim: Apple defines exactly two system sheet detents on iPhone — large (fully expanded height) and medium (about half of fully expanded height) — with large supported automatically; adding medium lets the sheet rest at both heights, while specifying only medium prevents full-height expansion. Custom detent values are also permitted. This is the authoritative source for the "bottom sheet" resting-height vocabulary and gives a concrete, checkable number (medium ≈ 50% of full height) rather than folklore.
claims.quote: Sheets resize according to their detents, which are particular heights at which a sheet naturally rests. Designed for iPhone, detents specify particular heights at which a sheet naturally rests. The system defines two detents: large is the height of a fully expanded sheet and medium is about half of the fully expanded height. Sheets can have one or more custom detent values. Sheets automatically support the large detent. Adding the medium detent allows the sheet to rest at both heights, whereas specifying only medium prevents the sheet from expanding to full height.

claims.claim: Apple prohibits stacked sheets: only one sheet may be displayed at a time from the main interface, and if an action inside a sheet triggers another sheet, the first must be closed before the second appears. The documented failure mode is disorientation — users expect closing a sheet to return them to the parent view, and landing on a second sheet makes them lose track of location.
claims.quote: Display only one sheet at a time from the main interface. When people close a sheet, they expect to return to the parent view or window. If closing a sheet takes people back to another sheet, they can lose track of where they are in your app. If something people do within a sheet results in another sheet appearing, close the first sheet before displaying the new one.

claims.claim: A resizable sheet must include a grabber — a small horizontal indicator at its top edge — which serves three functions: it signals draggability, it is tappable to cycle through detents, and it is exposed to VoiceOver so a sheet can be resized without sight. This makes the grabber an accessibility requirement, not decoration: resize affordance must exist in non-visual form.
claims.quote: Include a grabber in a resizable sheet. A grabber shows people that they can drag the sheet to resize it; they can also tap it to cycle through the detents. In addition to providing a visual indicator of resizability, a grabber also works with VoiceOver so people can resize the sheet without seeing the screen.

claims.claim: Apple explicitly rules sheets out for complex or prolonged flows and names the correct substitutes per platform: full-screen modal presentation on iOS/iPadOS for video, photos, camera, or multistep editing; a separate window or full-screen mode on macOS for self-contained tasks like document editing; and a Full Space in visionOS. This is a documented condition-of-use boundary between sheet, full-screen modal, and routed/separate surface.
claims.quote: For complex or prolonged user flows, consider alternatives to sheets. For example, iOS and iPadOS offer a full-screen style of modal view that can work well to display content like videos, photos, or camera views or to help people perform multistep tasks like document or photo editing. In a macOS experience, you might want to open a new window or let people enter full-screen mode instead of using a sheet.

claims.claim: Sheet dismissal must never depend on a Done button alone: Done must always be paired with a Cancel button (or a Back button for multi-step flows), and all three must not appear together. In iOS/iPadOS single-view sheets, Cancel goes on the leading edge of the top toolbar and Done on the trailing edge. Separately, swipe-to-dismiss is the expected gesture, and unsaved changes must trigger an action-sheet confirmation. (This button-placement guidance was revised 2026-03-24.)
claims.quote: Provide an alternative to the Done button. If you provide a Done button, always pair it with a Cancel button to give people a clear way to dismiss the sheet without confirming or saving their changes, or a Back button to move to a previous step in the sheet. Relying solely on the Done button implies that completing the task is the only way to exit the sheet, which can feel restrictive or misleading. Avoid showing all three buttons — Cancel, Done, and Back — together.

result.publishDate: Last updated 2026-03-24 (change-log note: "Updated guidance for button placement"); no original publication date given — HIG is a continuously revised document.

claims.claim: Color vision deficiency affects up to 8% of men and 0.5% of women (>4% of the population overall, ~600 million people worldwide), which is the quantitative basis for requiring CVD-safe palettes and non-color redundant encodings in any chart the pipeline ships.
claims.quote: CVD reduces the ability to distinguish between certain colors and affects up to 8% of men and 0.5% of women

claims.claim: Rainbow-style colormaps (jet) create false features: bright bands read as local maxima even where the underlying data value is lower, so jet misleads viewers with AND without CVD — a documented failure mode, not a style preference.
claims.quote: An example of how the data may be misinterpreted are evident in the bright yellow spots in (b) and (c), which appear to represent significantly higher values than the surrounding regions. However, in fact, the dark red (in b) and dark yellow (in c) actually represent the highest values.

claims.claim: Viridis is perceptually uniform and is the current default standard, but it is optimized for normal color vision and NOT for CVD; cividis is the paper's CVD-optimized replacement giving near-identical interpretation for red-green colorblind and non-CVD viewers. So 'we used viridis' is not sufficient evidence of a colorblind-safe sequential scale.
claims.quote: Right now, viridis is seen as the gold standard since it follows each of the design principles discussed above; however, it is optimal for those with normal vision and not CVD.

claims.claim: Perceptual uniformity is constructed by working in a perceptually uniform colorspace (here CIECAM02-UCS) where equal Euclidean distance equals equal perceived color difference, then converting to sRGB for display — the same principle behind OKLCH/OKLab scale construction, and it is a computable design criterion rather than a taste judgement.
claims.quote: Equal Euclidean distances between values in this space leads to an equal color difference perception, enabling the straightforward creation of perceptually uniform colormaps

claims.claim: Color carries vastly more discriminable levels than lightness alone — roughly ten million distinguishable colors versus about thirty shades of gray — which bounds how much quantitative resolution a monochrome or greyscale-only fallback rendering can convey.
claims.quote: Humans without CVD can distinguish around ten million different colors versus only about thirty shades of gray

claims.claim: Cleveland & McGill's perceptual ranking of encodings replicates on the web (crowdsourced, N=50/chart, 3,481 trials): position along a common scale is most accurate and significantly beats length, and area/circular-area and color-ish encodings sit at the bottom. BUT the folklore item that angle is worse than length was NOT supported — angle (pie) performed comparably to length in both this study and the 1984 original. Treat 'position > length > angle > area > color' as measured only at its endpoints; the angle-vs-length rung is unsupported.
claims.quote: The ranking of types by accuracy is consistent between the two experiments (Figure 4). Types 1 and 2 are closer in the crowdsourced study; this may be a result of a smaller display mitigating the effect of distance. Types 4 and 5 are more accurate than in the original study, but position encoding still significantly outperformed length encoding. ... Theory also suggests that angle should perform worse than length, but the results do not support this. Cleveland & McGill also did not find angle to perform worse than length, but as stated their position-angle results are not directly comparable to their position-length results.

claims.claim: Measured sizing threshold for micro-charts/sparklines: judgment accuracy plateaus above ~80 pixels of chart height on a 0-100 scale; charts only 40px tall produce significantly more error (p < 0.001), while 80, 160 and 320px are statistically indistinguishable. So a sparkline or in-line micro-chart can be shrunk to ~80px tall with no measured accuracy cost, but 40px is measurably too small. 2 (chart type) x 3 (height) x 4 (gridline spacing) factorial, 2,880 responses, ANOVA F(3,2802)=14.16, p<0.001 for height.
claims.quote: charts 40 pixels tall resulted in significantly more error (p < 0.001 in all cases), but found no significant difference between the other heights. The results confirm our hypothesis that accuracy plateaus as chart heights increase, and suggest little benefit for increasing chart height beyond 80 pixels when using a 0-100 scale. This size roughly coincides with the point at which the pixel and data resolutions match.

claims.claim: Gridlines measurably improve value-comparison accuracy, but only if they are spaced at least 8 pixels apart; densely packed gridlines (10-unit spacing in a 40px-tall chart) degrade accuracy by impeding label reading. This is a concrete, checkable rule for hairline rules and axis grids in dense chart and table design. Gridline spacing main effect F(3,2802)=31.98, p<0.001; height x spacing interaction F(9,2802)=2.11, p<0.026.
claims.quote: Adding gridlines improved accuracy, though post-hoc tests found no significant difference between 10 and 20 gridlines (p = 0.887) or between 50 and 100 (p = 0.905). Error increased steeply in charts with a height of 40 pixels and gridline spacing of 10 units. Presumably the dense packing of gridlines impedes accurate tracing of their labels. The results suggest that gridlines be separated by at least 8 pixels.

claims.claim: Rectangles with a 1:1 aspect ratio are the WORST case for area comparison — worse than non-square aspect ratios — a result robust across both plain-rectangle and treemap display conditions (p < 0.05 effect of aspect ratio; 108 unique trials, 2x9 factorial, 6 replications). This directly undercuts 'squarified' treemap layouts, whose optimization objective is to push rectangles toward 1:1. Proposed mechanism: viewers substitute 1D side-length comparison for area, which is maximally ambiguous when sides are equal.
claims.quote: We found a significant (p < 0.05) effect of aspect ratio on judgment accuracy, as shown in Figure 5. Somewhat surprisingly, comparisons of rectangles with aspect ratio 1 exhibited the worst performance, a result robust across both the rectangle and treemap display conditions. This finding suggests that viewers actually benefit from the inability of a squarified treemap algorithm to perfectly optimize the rectangles to 1:1 aspect ratios. The result is consistent with the hypothesis that viewers use 1D length comparisons to help estimate area: comparing the lengths of sides as a proxy for area leads to maximal error when comparing squares.

claims.claim: Gridline transparency: alpha = 0.2 is corroborated as a safe default for gridlines/reference elements across background lightness and plot density. Plot density significantly affects the preferred alpha (F(3,2413)=3.49, p=0.015) but background intensity does not (F(4,2413)=0.44, p=0.779). Web-user displays also skew the result: OS/monitor gamma has a significant effect (F(1,1391)=10.24, p<0.001), with pre-10.6 macOS users choosing darker alphas — i.e. a single-lab-monitor calibration under-represents real viewers.
claims.quote: Applying analysis of variance, we found a significant effect of plot density (F(3,2413) = 3.49, p = 0.015) but not of background intensity (F(4,2413) = 0.44, p = 0.779), consistent with Stone & Bartram's findings. ... Our results corroborate Stone & Bartram's recommendation of alpha = 0.2 as a "safe" default.

claims.claim: Non-perceptually-uniform colour maps (rainbow/jet) cause a reader's visual interpretation to diverge from the objective data by more than 7% of the displayed data variation — a measured distortion figure, not folklore, and the strongest available argument for banning rainbow scales in the pipeline's chart vocabulary.
claims.quote: Such a colour-introduced blind interpretation can diverge from an objective representation by more than seven percent of the displayed data variation.

claims.claim: Colour-vision deficiency affects 8% of men and 0.5% of women worldwide, so any chart encoding meaning in red-versus-green at similar lightness is unreadable to a large fraction of readers — this makes non-colour redundant encoding an accessibility requirement, not a nicety.
claims.quote: worldwide 0.5% of women and 8% of men are subject to a colour-vision deficiency (CVD)

claims.claim: A monotonic lightness gradient is the single property that makes a colour scale survive greyscale conversion while remaining perceptually uniform and ordered — i.e. lightness, not hue, is the load-bearing channel, which is directly testable by desaturating any generated chart.
claims.quote: With an even, monotonic lightness gradient, a colour palette remains readable (as well as perceptually uniform and ordered) even after a conversion to grey scale, assuming no complicated grey-scale filter is used.

claims.claim: Scale-type selection is determined by the data's structure, not aesthetics: data divergent about a central value requires a diverging or multi-sequential map that distinguishes both sides of the axis — a falsifiable selection rule for the pipeline's missing colour-scale vocabulary.
claims.quote: If the data is divergent about a central value (e.g., centred about zero), a divergent or a multi-sequential colour map should be chosen that clearly and intuitively distinguishes either side of the axis.

claims.claim: The authors state that rainbow-style distorting colour maps are resurging in scientific publishing despite communities having moved away from them — supporting the pipeline's anti-cliché rule that rainbow/jet reads as a default-tool artefact rather than a design choice. Note: asserted qualitatively, backed only by a cited conference blog count, not a systematic survey.
claims.quote: Although some scientific communities have largely moved away from using distorting colour maps, such as rainbow, there are numerous signs of bad habits returning en masse.

claims.claim: ColorBrewer caps schemes at 12 classes but the authors state only a few schemes stay differentiable at that count; many sequential sets stop at 9 because further subdivision is "perceptually unreliable", and the stated practitioner rule of thumb is that cartographers seldom exceed seven classes on a choropleth — with the exception that isoline maps or maps with very regular spatial patterns can safely exceed seven. This is an attributable (if rule-of-thumb rather than experimentally measured) ceiling on how many colour steps a sequential/diverging encoding can carry.
claims.quote: These sets have been designed to produce attractive colour schemes of similar appearance for maps ranging from 3 to 12 classes. Not all colour schemes can be expanded to 12 classes, and many of the sequential scheme sets, for example, stop at 9 classes because further divisions within the scheme are perceptually unreliable (Figure 2). […] The maximum number of data classes ColorBrewer supports is 12, although only a few of the colour schemes can be divided into this many steps and remain differentiable. As a general rule of thumb, cartographers seldom use more than seven classes on a choropleth map. Isoline maps, or choropleth maps with very regular spatial patterns, can safely use more than seven data classes because similar colours are seen next to each other, making them easier to distinguish.

claims.claim: Colour-vision safety is a property of scheme TYPE, not of individual palettes: all sequential schemes are usable by red-green colour-impaired readers because they carry visible lightness differences; almost all qualitative schemes are NOT; diverging schemes were deliberately hue-paired for colour-blind readers except red-yellow-green and full-spectral ones.
