The authors also flag the provenance of this judgement as approximate — theory plus a single red-green-impaired evaluator, not a formal study.
claims.quote: Generally, the hue pairs for diverging schemes were selected to accommodate colour-blind readers, with the exception of red-yellow-green and full spectral schemes. Almost all of the qualitative schemes are difficult for colour-blind readers and all of the sequential schemes are useful to them, because they include visible lightness differences. […] These approximate evaluations were made using both a theoretical understanding of colour-blind confusions throughout colour space (Olson and Brewer, 1997) as well as an evaluation of the schemes by an individual with red-green colour impairment, although we would like to see more thorough testing of the schemes to confirm that they accommodate a wide range of colour vision impairments.

claims.claim: The three-way taxonomy is a data-type matching rule with concrete construction constraints: sequential = ordinal/numeric low-to-high, lightness-dominant, "dark equals more" as cartographic convention; diverging = a critical break (mean, median or zero) marked by hue AND lightness change, always multi-hue; qualitative = nominal, hue varied with saturation and lightness held near-constant, and mixing neon with pastel in one categorical palette is explicitly discouraged because the saturation variation implies a false order.
claims.quote: Sequential colour schemes (Figure 3a) imply order and are suited to representing data that ranges from low-to-high values either on an ordinal scale (e.g. cold, warm, hot) or on a numerical scale […] Lightness steps dominate the look of these schemes, usually with light colours for low data values and dark colours for high values. 'Dark equals more' is a standard cartographic convention. […] Diverging colour schemes (Figure 3b) should be used when a critical data class or break point needs to be emphasized. The break or class in the middle of the sequence is emphasized by a hue and lightness change and should represent a critical value in the data such as the mean, median or zero. […] Qualitative schemes work best when hue is varied and saturation and lightness are kept or nearly constant. We do not recommend arbitrarily using strong 'neon' colours (i.e. high saturation) and pastel colours (i.e. light and low saturation) in the same qualitative colour scheme because these variations in saturation might imply order.

claims.claim: A palette that reads correctly in an ordered legend can fail in the actual graphic: simultaneous contrast makes a mid-lightness region surrounded by dark regions look lighter than it is, and separated light outliers become mutually indistinguishable. The authors state as a general rule that a scheme fails in the randomly-arranged portion of a map before it fails in the ordered portion — i.e. palettes must be validated against the real spatial arrangement of marks, not against a swatch strip.
claims.quote: A well-known problem with choropleth maps is simultaneous contrast (Brewer, 1997). For example, a single enumeration unit (e.g. county) of medium lightness that is surrounded by dark enumeration units will appear lighter than it actually is. Thus, the map-reader will not be able to accurately match these outlying enumeration units with colours in the legend […] As a general rule, the more complex the spatial patterns of the maps, the harder it will be to distinguish slightly different colours. To illustrate this, the maps in ColorBrewer present colours as both random distributions and well-ordered distributions (sequential banding). All other things being equal, a colour scheme will fail to be fully differentiable in the random portion of the map before it fails in the ordered portion.

claims.claim: ColorBrewer's schemes were NOT generated in a perceptually uniform colour space — they were hand-designed as arcs across the outer shell of colour space using CMYK/Munsell knowledge, then validated by eye across eight output devices (2 CRTs, 2 laptop LCDs, 2 LCD projectors, colour and B&W laser printers), with failures flagged by icon. A specific documented failure mode: diverging schemes do not survive greyscale reproduction, because photocopies capture only lightness and diverging schemes vary lightness symmetrically about the midpoint.
claims.quote: For this project both the sequential and diverging schemes were constructed from conceptual arcs across the outer shell of colour space. Colours were chosen that are well saturated and organized in orderly lightness sequences. The scheme was not designed using perceptual colour specifications, but knowledge of the relationships between CMYK colour mixture (cyan, magenta, yellow and black) and perceptually ordered colour spaces were used, such as Munsell (Brewer, 1989) […] Diverging schemes are always multi-hue sequences and, because of the way in which lightness is varied, do not make good black and white photocopies or prints (which only capture differences in lightness). […] We examined each of the colour scheme sets using two CRT screens (Mac and PC), two laptop LCD screens (old and new), two LCD projectors (old and new), and prints from a Tektronix colour laser printer and a black-and-white laser printer. We evaluated the schemes by deciding whether we could differentiate all of the colours on the multiple backgrounds offered in the ColorBrewer map display.

result.publishDate: 2003-06 (The Cartographic Journal, Vol. 40 No. 1, pp. 27-37, June 2003)

claims.claim: Core Web Vitals sets LCP 'good' at ≤2.5s and 'poor' at >4s, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads — the 75th percentile chosen so that 3 of 4 visits met the target and to limit outlier influence. This is the authoritative anchor for the pipeline's own 'LCP under 1.5s' shell budget (the budget is stricter than the standard, so it is safely conservative).
claims.quote: By using the 75th percentile, we know that most visits to the site (3 of 4) experienced the target level of performance or better. Additionally, the 75th percentile value is less likely to be affected by outliers.

claims.claim: The LCP 2.5s threshold is grounded in classic HCI response-time research, not invented: Newell's ~1s 'immediate response' band (0.3–3s) and Miller's finding that task character degrades past two seconds. So the commonly cited 'about 1 second feels immediate / 2 seconds is the tolerance edge' numbers are measured research, not folklore.
claims.quote: Responses that must be made to some stimulus within _very approximately one second_ (that is, roughly from ~0.3sec to ~3sec).

claims.claim: INP 'good' is ≤200ms and 'poor' is >500ms, and the 100–200ms band is justified by Michotte's 1962 perception-of-causality work (delays up to ~100ms read as A causing B; 100–200ms is mixed) plus Kaaresoja's virtual-button study where ≤85ms visual feedback was judged simultaneous with the press 75% of the time. This gives attributable numbers for micro-interaction feedback timing (hover/press/state-change response), not just designer folklore.
claims.quote: When the delay between button press and visual feedback was 85ms or less, participants reported the visual feedback appeared simultaneously with the button press 75% of the time.

claims.claim: The CLS thresholds (0.1 good / 0.25 poor) are explicitly NOT derived from published research — Google states no relevant research existed and set them by internally evaluating real pages, finding shift ≥0.15 consistently perceived as disruptive. Any claim that 0.1 CLS is a research-validated perceptual limit is therefore overstated; it is an internal qualitative judgement.
claims.quote: CLS is new, we are not aware of research that can directly inform the thresholds for this metric.

claims.claim: Thresholds are constrained by an explicit achievability rule — a 'good' threshold is only adopted if at least 10% of existing origins already meet it, and 'poor' is by default the worst-performing 10–30% of origins. This means CWV cutoffs encode what the web currently achieves, not an ideal ceiling, so a design pipeline can legitimately set stricter internal budgets.
claims.quote: To confirm that a threshold is achievable, we require that at least 10% of origins meet the 'good' threshold.

claims.claim: In a controlled three-condition comparison (n=136) with loading animations of identical duration, the skeleton screen lost to both the loading spinner and a plain blank screen on every measured metric — directly contradicting the widespread claim that skeleton screens improve perceived performance.
claims.quote: the skeleton screen performed the worst by all metrics.

claims.claim: Measured values: participants estimated the wait as 2.82s with a skeleton screen vs 2.41s with a spinner and 2.29s with a blank screen; 59% of the skeleton group agreed loading was quick vs 74% (spinner) and 66% (blank); post-load task completion took 10.54s (skeleton) vs 9.49s (spinner) and 9.50s (blank). These are measured numbers, not folklore, and they rank the spinner ahead of the skeleton.
claims.quote: Agreed loading was quick — Skeleton 59%, Spinner 74%, Blank 66%. Average perceived wait (seconds) — Skeleton 2.82, Spinner 2.41, Blank 2.29. Task completion time (seconds) — Skeleton 10.54, Spinner 9.49, Blank 9.50.

claims.claim: The authors name three boundary conditions under which skeletons should still win — familiar interfaces, very short waits, and non-novelty — which is the usable 'Right when' condition: a skeleton earns its place only when the user already knows the layout it is standing in for and the wait is sub-second-ish, not on a first-visit portfolio shell.
claims.quote: Skeleton screens work better in familiar interfaces and can be off-putting in new settings when users don't know what to expect. ... Skeleton screens work best when wait times are very short.

claims.claim: The authors explicitly decline to treat the result as settled and report no statistical significance testing; group sizes were unequal (39 skeleton / 39 spinner / 58 blank) and roughly half of participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk — so the finding is indicative evidence against the skeleton-screen default, not an established effect size.
claims.quote: Our hunch is that each of these reasons has some merit, but more testing is needed to know for certain.

claims.claim: The study's stated design recommendation is conditional use rather than adoption-by-default, despite skeletons being shipped by Google, Medium and Slack — i.e. 'everyone uses it' is not evidence of perceived-performance benefit.
claims.quote: skeleton screens aren't a silver bullet for increasing perceived performance and should be used thoughtfully.

claims.claim: NN/g prescribes a three-tier duration rule for loading feedback: no indicator below ~1 second, a looped/indeterminate animation for waits of 2–10 seconds, and a percent-done (determinate) progress bar for waits of 10 seconds or longer. This gives the pipeline a defensible, attributable numeric rule for choosing between spinner and progress bar rather than folklore.
claims.quote: "Use a progress indicator for any action that takes longer than about 1.0 second" ... "This indicator should be reserved for actions that take between 2-10 seconds." ... "Generally, percent-done progress indicators should be used for longer processes that take 10 or more seconds."

claims.claim: Showing a moving progress bar makes users willing to wait on average 3 times longer than with no progress indicator, and produces higher satisfaction — a measured effect from a peer-reviewed study (Nah, F., 2004, Behaviour & Information Technology 23(3)) at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, not a folklore number.
claims.quote: The researchers found that the people who saw the moving feedback bar experienced higher satisfaction and were willing to wait on average 3 times longer than those who did not see any progress indicators.

claims.claim: For operations completing in under 1 second, adding a looped animation is actively harmful (distracting) rather than neutral — so a shell that paints in under 1.5s should generally show no spinner at all on its critical path.
claims.quote: For anything that takes less than 1 second to load, it is distracting to use a looped animation

claims.claim: Static (non-animated) indicators are insufficient as loading feedback and must be replaced with an animated or determinate indicator, because they carry no information about ongoing progress. This constrains the 'designed reduced-motion still' requirement: a frozen spinner is not an acceptable reduced-motion fallback; the still must encode progress some other way (e.g. text percentage, stepped bar).
claims.quote: Static indicators should be replaced with another type of indicator, because they do not offer enough information about what is happening.

claims.claim: The mechanism by which progress indicators improve waiting is attentional: they consume cognitive resources that would otherwise be spent monitoring the wait, thereby reducing the user's perception of elapsed time — which is the stated rationale for investing in designed preloaders over bare delays.
claims.quote: They can reduce users' perception of time: Users devote some cognitive resources to the feedback itself, and they pay less attention to the wait itself.

claims.claim: CSS Color 4 normatively makes Oklab the default interpolation color space when a host syntax (gradients, transitions, filters, color-mix(), relative color syntax) does not specify one — with an explicit legacy carve-out that hex/named/rgb()/hsl()/hwb() colors must still interpolate in gamma-encoded sRGB, and that authors opt into the better behaviour by writing at least one endpoint as color(srgb r g b) or by naming the interpolation space. This is directly implementable and zero-byte (no runtime), and it means a portfolio's gradients/state transitions get perceptually even ramps only if the author avoids legacy sRGB syntax.
claims.quote: If the host syntax does not define what color space interpolation should take place in, it defaults to Oklab. […] However, user agents must handle interpolation between legacy sRGB color formats (hex colors, named colors, rgb(), hsl() or hwb() and the equivalent alpha-including forms) in gamma-encoded sRGB space. This provides Web compatibility; legacy sRGB content interpolates in the sRGB space by default. […] This also means that authors can choose to opt-in to better interpolation, even between sRGB colors, by using the non-legacy color(srgb r g b) form for at least one of their colors, or by explicitly specifying an interpolation color space.

claims.claim: The spec states the provenance and the specific perceptual advantages of Oklab over CIE Lab/LCH: it was derived by numerical optimization over a dataset of visually similar colors and has improved hue linearity, hue uniformity and chroma uniformity — the technical justification for building sequential/diverging data-visualization scales in OKLCH rather than HSL or sRGB.
claims.quote: Recently, Oklab, an improved Lab-like space has been developed [Oklab]. The corresponding polar form is called OkLCh. It was produced by numerical optimization of a large dataset of visually similar colors, and has improved hue linearity, hue uniformity, and chroma uniformity compared to CIE LCH.

claims.claim: The spec gives an explicit decision rule for which interpolation space fits which task — linear-light spaces (CIE XYZ, srgb-linear, display-p3-linear) for physical light mixing, Oklab/Lab when steps must be perceptually even (e.g. a gradient or a sequential ramp), OkLCh/LCH when chroma must be maximised through a transition, and sRGB only for legacy compatibility — and explicitly names sRGB's failure mode as overly dark or greyish mixes.
claims.quote: If colors need to be evenly spaced perceptually (such as in a gradient), the Oklab color space (and the older Lab), are designed to be perceptually uniform. If avoiding graying out in color mixing is desired, i.e. maximizing chroma throughout the transition, OkLCh (and the older LCH) work well for that. Lastly, compatibility with legacy Web content may be the most important consideration. The sRGB color space, which is neither linear-light nor perceptually uniform, is the choice here, even though it produces poorer results (overly dark or greyish mixes).

claims.claim: Interpolation of non-opaque colors is specified to happen on premultiplied components, with hue exempt in cylindrical spaces, and the default hue arc is `shorter` unless the host syntax says otherwise — so a fade-to-transparent gradient does not pass through grey, and a two-stop OKLCH gradient takes the short way round the hue wheel by default (use `in oklch longer hue` to force the long arc).
claims.quote: For rectangular orthogonal color coordinate systems, all component values are multiplied by the alpha value. For cylindrical polar color coordinate systems, the hue angle is not premultiplied, but the other two axes are premultiplied. […] Unless otherwise specified, if no specific hue interpolation algorithm is selected by the host syntax, the default is shorter.

claims.claim: Because Oklab is more perceptually uniform than CIE Lab, the spec defines colour difference in it (ΔEOK) as plain Euclidean distance in 3D — root sum of squares of the L, a, b deltas — which is a cheap, implementable test for checking that a categorical palette's swatches are perceptually distinct (and by extension for validating colourblind-safe separations) without a ΔE2000 implementation.
claims.quote: Because Oklab is more perceptually uniform than CIE Lab, the color difference is a straightforward distance in 3D space (root sum of squares). Although trivial, a sample implementation is give in § 20.2 ΔEOK.

claims.claim: AI-default web design has a specific, nameable palette-and-type signature: cream/beige backgrounds, rusty-orange accents, large italicized-and-highlighted serif display type, and letter-spaced ("tracked out") subheadings. This is a concrete, checkable list of visual tells the portfolio pipeline must blacklist to satisfy its anti-template rule.
claims.quote: beige- and cream-colored backgrounds, rusty orange-hued accents, and large serif typefaces that are italicized and highlighted … Subheadings are often "tracked out," in design parlance, with spaces between the letters

claims.claim: A specific component-level cliché is attributed to Claude output: dashboard tiles built from multiple nested rounded-rectangle outlines with a neon glow beneath. This is a named container/card failure mode — directly relevant to the repo's missing component-pattern vocabulary and to what now reads as AI-default.
claims.quote: Claude often creates dashboard elements with multiple rounded rectangular outlines, sometimes with a neon glow underneath

claims.claim: Ticker-like scrolling text bars (marquee strips styled like cable-news chyrons) are a recurring AI-generated-site tell, i.e. a motion/typographic technique that has become generic rather than distinctive.
claims.quote: prevalence of ticker-like text bars, as if the website were a cable-news show

claims.claim: There is a reputational penalty, not just an aesthetic one: design-literate viewers can recognize the AI-generic look on sight and react negatively to the site as a whole. This makes avoiding the listed tells a functional requirement for a portfolio site, not a taste preference.
claims.quote: The second the informed viewer realizes that you fell for the AI generic, they're turned off.

claims.claim: The AI-generic warm/mid-century palette has become tainted by association for at least some designers, who report aversion to a palette family they otherwise like — evidence that the genericness attaches to the palette itself, independent of execution quality.
claims.quote: Now I find myself instinctively repulsed by the warm tones even though I love this kind of color palette.

claims.claim: Skeleton screens work (when they work) via the active-vs-passive waiting mechanism, not because gray boxes are inherently better than spinners: a spinner keeps the entire wait passive, while each state change in a skeleton flips the user briefly back into active waiting, and time-perception research finds active waits are perceived as shorter than passive ones (Kadlec cites the JSTOR-hosted time-perception literature at jstor.org/stable/171439).
claims.quote: According to research on time perception , active waiting periods are perceived as faster than passive waiting phases. With a progress bar or spinner, our entire waiting period is passive: there's nothing for us to do but watch this spinner that has absolutely nothing to do with the content we're about to see.

claims.claim: The perceived-performance benefit of active waiting decays as total wait length grows, so a skeleton screen cannot rescue a multi-second delay; Kadlec cites Scott Jehl's measurement of desktop YouTube showing 6.9 seconds of gray boxes on a cable connection as an example that is far past the useful window.
claims.quote: In that example, as tested on a Cable connection, we're staring at gray boxes for 6.9 seconds before we get to see the content. That's far too long of a delay to expect a few gray boxes to hold us over…

claims.claim: A skeleton is only effective if it fills in incrementally through multiple stages (Polar's three: gray boxes+borders+headings → text → imagery); the common two-stage implementation (gray boxes → everything at once) drops the user back into passive waiting for the majority of the delay and reads as bad UX.
claims.quote: Looking back at the YouTube example, we have two basic stages (pretty typical for many skeleton UI's we see implemented today): Gray boxes and borders / All the things! … we're going to switch right back into a passive waiting state for the rest of that duration.

claims.claim: A skeleton screen must geometrically predict the final layout; if the real content shifts the boxes (e.g. YouTube's skeleton reflowing when an ad loads), the misleading expectation costs more than the perceived-performance gain — making layout-shift avoidance a correctness requirement of the pattern, not a polish item.
claims.quote: we were given expectations of what content would be displayed and where, and those expectations ended up being misleading. We now have to re-orient ourselves to where the content ends up being displayed. When the skeleton screen doesn't match the outcome, we've created confusion and frustration that will overcome any benefit you might have gotten

claims.claim: Skeleton screens are a workaround whose effectiveness is expected to erode through familiarity/conditioning as the pattern becomes ubiquitous — i.e. the pattern's benefit is not a fixed property but decays with user exposure, and the first-choice fix is removing the delay.
claims.quote: As the pattern of skeleton screens becomes increasingly familiar, the ability it has to switch us into that active state of waiting is going to decrease. If we're trying to use this approach as a band-aid for long loading times that users have to encounter every time they use our site, it's going to fall on its face pretty quickly.

claims.claim: Cleveland & McGill establish the canonical perceptual ranking of visual encodings as six accuracy tiers, most-to-least accurate: (1) position along a common scale, (2) position along nonaligned scales, (3) length/direction/angle, (4) area, (5) volume/curvature, (6) shading/color saturation. Ties within tiers 3, 5 and 6 are explicitly unresolved — the paper states there was not enough information to separate them. The accompanying design rule is to encode using the highest tier available. Note this ranking is HYPOTHESIZED from psychophysics plus prior work, and only tiers 1 vs 2 vs 3 were experimentally tested in this paper; area, volume and color rankings are theoretical here, not measured.
claims.quote: The following are the 10 elementary tasks in Figure 1, ordered from most to least accurate: 1. Position along a common scale 2. Positions along nonaligned scales 3. Length, direction, angle 4. Area 5. Volume, curvature 6. Shading, color saturation ... Three of the ranks—3, 5, and 6—have more than one task; at the moment there is not enough information to separate the ties. ... The theory provides a guideline for graph construction: Graphs should employ elementary tasks as high in the ordering as possible.

claims.claim: The accuracy advantage of position over length and angle is MEASURED, not folklore: two controlled experiments (51 subjects with usable data each, judging bar charts and pie charts on 'what percentage is one value of a larger value') found position judgments more accurate than length judgments by factors of 1.4 to 2.5, and 1.96 times as accurate as angle judgments. These are the specific numbers to attribute when claiming position beats angle — i.e. bar chart beats pie chart by roughly a factor of 2.
claims.quote: In both experiments there were 51 subjects with usable data. ... In the first experiment, position judgments were more accurate than length judgments by factors varying from 1.4 to 2.5. In the second experiment, position judgments were 1.96 times as accurate as angle judgments.

claims.claim: Gross failure, not just average error, is far more frequent for lower-tier encodings: large errors (log error > 4) occurred 5.3x more often for length judgments than position judgments (136 of 2,550 judgments), and 7.3x more often for angle judgments than position judgments (219 of 4,080 judgments). Encoding choice therefore governs catastrophic misreading rate, not merely precision — a stronger argument against pie/angle encodings than the mean-accuracy factor alone.
claims.quote: Of the 2,550 judgments made by the subjects, 136 had a log error greater than 4. ... Seventy-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the length judgments; since there were three position judgments for each two length judgments, the rate of occurrence of large errors for length judgments is 5.3 times that for position judgments. ... in this experiment 219 of the 4,080 judgments had large errors. Eighty-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the angle judgments; thus the rate of occurrence of large errors for the angle judgments is 7.3 times that for the position judgments.

claims.claim: The paper's applied conclusion is that pie charts, divided bar charts, and shaded statistical maps (choropleths) are not fixable by refinement and should be REPLACED, and it names three specific replacement forms: dot charts, dot charts with grouping, and framed-rectangle charts. Choropleth shading is condemned because shading/color saturation sits in the LAST accuracy tier. Length and angle judgments also carry consistent bias: subjects systematically underestimate when true percentages fall in the 25-50 range.
claims.quote: The conclusion is that radical surgery on these popular graphs is needed, and as replacements we offer alternative graphical forms—dot charts, dot charts with grouping, and framed-rectangle charts. ... An important part of the contribution to the errors for length and angle judgments is consistent bias. When the true percentages are in the range of 25–50%, subjects tend to underestimate values for these types of judgments.

claims.claim: The 'framed rectangle' is the paper's concrete mechanism for upgrading an encoding one tier: surrounding equal-width bars with frames of equal size and construction converts the task from judging LENGTH (tier 3) to judging POSITION ALONG NONALIGNED SCALES (tier 2), making otherwise-imperceptible differences visible. The justification is Weber's Law — the unfilled remainder of the frame is short when the filled bars are long and similar, so the percentage difference between the short unfilled bars is much greater than between the long filled bars. This is a cheap, purely geometric technique (an SVG/CSS-native swap for choropleth shading, which the paper applies to statistical maps in Section 5.3).
claims.quote: Each symbol, called a framed rectangle, is actually a little graph with a scale and with one number portrayed. The elementary perceptual task is judging position along nonaligned scales, and now we can easily see that the right bar represents a larger quantity than the left. ... Suppose two framed rectangles have filled bars that are long and close in length, such as in the bottom of Figure 12. Then the percentage difference of the lengths of the unfilled bars is much greater than that of the filled bars; by Weber's Law one can much more readily detect a difference in the short unfilled bars than in the long filled bars. Thus it is the unfilled bars in the bottom of Figure 12 that allow perception of a difference that is not perceptible in the top.

claims.claim: Material Design 3's easing-and-duration system is officially deprecated in favour of a spring-based 'motion physics' system introduced in the M3 Expressive update; the duration/easing token set is retained only for transitions and is explicitly no longer maintained. This is direct platform-vendor evidence for the 'springs vs. duration-and-easing' question — the largest design system in the world has moved its default to springs.
claims.quote: In the expressive update, components and motion now use the motion physics system, which uses springs. Products should migrate to the new system. The easing and duration system is still used for transitions and can be used by teams that haven't yet updated to GM3 Expressive, but is no longer maintained.

claims.claim: M3 publishes an exact 16-step duration token scale in milliseconds, keyed to the spatial scope of the transition rather than to taste: short1-4 = 50/100/150/200ms ('small utility-focused transitions'), medium1-4 = 250/300/350/400ms ('transitions that traverse a medium area of the screen'), long1-4 = 450/500/550/600ms ('large expressive transitions'), extra-long1-4 = 700/800/900/1000ms (above 600ms, 'rare'). These are attributable platform-guidance numbers, not folklore, and they give a defensible rule: duration scales with distance travelled and area covered.
claims.quote: Short durations — These are used for small utility-focused transitions. […] Medium durations — These are used for transitions that traverse a medium area of the screen. […] Long durations — These durations are often paired with Emphasized easing. They're used for large expressive transitions. […] Extra long durations — Though rare, some transitions use durations above 600ms. These are usually used for ambient transitions that don't involve user input.

claims.claim: M3's flagship 'Emphasized' easing curve has NO CSS equivalent and the spec instructs web implementers to fall back to Standard easing; only the decelerate/accelerate variants are expressible as a single cubic-bezier. The Android definition is a two-segment path — pathInterpolator(M 0,0 C 0.05,0, 0.133333,0.06, 0.166666,0.4 C 0.208333,0.82, 0.25,1, 1,1) — which a single cubic-bezier() cannot represent, so on the web it requires CSS linear() sampling, an SVG/JS driver, or the documented downgrade. This is a concrete web-native implementability constraint.
claims.quote: CSS | N/A (Use Standard as a fallback) | cubic-bezier(0.05, 0.7, 0.1, 1.0) | cubic-bezier(0.3, 0.0, 0.8, 0.15)

claims.claim: M3 gives exact, copy-pasteable CSS values for the Standard easing set — standard = cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.0, 0, 1.0), standard decelerate = cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0, 1), standard accelerate = cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 1, 1) — and scopes them to 'simple, small, or utility-focused transitions', while the Emphasized set is scoped as the expressive default. The accelerate/decelerate split encodes the entering-vs-exiting rule: decelerate (fast start, slow settle) for elements entering the screen, accelerate for elements leaving.
claims.quote: Standard easing set — This set is used for simple, small, or utility-focused transitions. […] CSS: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.0, 0, 1.0); cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0, 1); cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 1, 1); […] Emphasized easing set — This set is the most common because it captures the expressive style of M3.

claims.claim: M3 anchors its duration scale with named component examples that map directly to the pipeline's card/drawer/sheet vocabulary: selection controls 200ms + Standard; a FAB expanding into a Sheet 400ms + Emphasized; a Card expanding to full screen 500ms + Emphasized; an ambient carousel auto-advance 1000ms + Emphasized. These give per-pattern timing defaults for container-transform and disclosure motion rather than a single global duration.
claims.quote: Selection controls have a short duration of 200ms with Standard easing […] A FAB expanding into a Sheet uses a 400ms duration with Emphasized easing […] A Card expanding to full screen uses a long 500ms duration with Emphasized easing […] An ambient carousel auto-advance transition uses an extra long 1000ms duration with emphasized easing

claims.claim: Bento grid layout has become the ubiquitous default in 2026 web design, and its ubiquity has itself spawned a named counter-movement — 'anti-grid brutalism' (deliberately broken layouts, raw HTML aesthetics, brutalist typography, monospace everything) — exemplified by The Browser Company's marketing pages and the v0.dev landing page. This is directly usable as an emerging-style entry AND as a named cliché to avoid.
claims.quote: deliberately broken layouts, raw HTML aesthetics, brutalist typography, monospace everything … When everyone else looks like Apple, looking different becomes the differentiator … The pendulum swung from custom to template back to custom, and now it is swinging from polished bento to deliberately raw brutalism.

claims.claim: A single Spline/WebGL hero scene costs 800kB–2MB of JavaScript runtime before first paint, collapsing Lighthouse and Core Web Vitals and causing 4G mobile users to abandon before load — so WebGL heroes are only defensible when the brand IS the experience (creative agencies, fashion houses, art portfolios). Number is the author's own unsourced estimate, not measured or externally cited.
claims.quote: single Spline scene in the hero loads 800kB to 2MB of JavaScript runtime before the user sees anything … Lighthouse scores collapse. Core Web Vitals fail. Mobile users on 4G drop the page … when the brand is the experience (creative agencies, fashion houses, art portfolios)

claims.claim: Glassmorphism's backdrop-filter: blur() causes 15–30% FPS drops, especially on Android, so it survives only in restrained form — acceptable on navigation bars, modals and feature cards, not on hero sections. The 15–30% figure is proprietary StudioMeyer client measurement with no third-party validation or methodology given.
claims.quote: computationally expensive, especially on Android … 15 to 30 percent FPS drops … survived in a more restrained form … navigation bars, modals and feature cards

claims.claim: Kinetic typography's documented failure mode is threefold and accessibility-relevant: it fights screen readers, fights search crawlers, and introduces layout shift that damages Core Web Vitals — restricting it to hero headlines and section transitions rather than a default pattern.
claims.quote: fights screen readers, fights search crawlers, and adds layout shift that destroys Core Web Vitals scores … sparingly, on hero headlines and section transitions

claims.claim: Organic blob shapes and asymmetric containers show a measurable gap between trend coverage and shipped work: they appear on brand-led landing pages but rarely ship on B2B SaaS, e-commerce, or any conversion-critical flow — giving a concrete 'Right when' condition (brand-first contexts only).
claims.quote: gap between trend articles and shipping reality … landing pages where the brand can afford the playfulness … B2B SaaS, e-commerce or any conversion-critical flow

claims.claim: The study found NO statistically significant difference between skeleton screens and spinners on any measured comparison. This is the most-cited primary experiment behind the design-industry claim that skeleton screens improve perceived performance (NN/g's "Skeleton Screens 101" cites it), so that guidance should be flagged in the repo as directional folklore rather than a measured effect — the source it rests on explicitly reports null results.
claims.quote: The results of this paper cannot show any significant differences in any of the comparisons between the web pages.

claims.claim: Directionally (means only, not significant), the skeleton-screen variant scored higher than the spinner variant on BOTH self-reported perceived loading speed and self-reported ease of navigation — i.e. the effect, if real, is on subjective perception and covers navigation legibility, not just speed.
claims.quote: The results show that the page using skeleton screens, scored higher on average on both perceived speed and ease of navigation.

claims.claim: Objective task performance ran OPPOSITE to subjective perception: participants on the spinner version were faster at completing the task (locating a specified article) on first visit to the site. Skeleton screens therefore may trade measured first-visit task speed for perceived speed — a documented failure mode for the pattern, likely because greyed placeholder blocks obscure the real information scent during scanning.
claims.quote: However, people using the page with spinners were faster at finding the article when entering the site for the first time.

claims.claim: The evidence base is a small between-variants usability test of a single fictional news site, combining a questionnaire with task-completion timing — a 4-page ECCE'18 short paper (9 citations as of retrieval). The design is underpowered and single-domain, which explains the null result and means it cannot be cited as evidence that skeletons are equivalent to spinners either; it is inconclusive in both directions.
claims.quote: This is done user testing a fictional news site with two variations, one showing skeleton screens before content is loaded, and another utilizing spinners. Both a questionnaire and measuring timing while finding a specified article when entering a website for the first time was used.

claims.claim: As of 2018 the paper positions progress bars and spinners as the established convention and skeleton screens as the newer trend — useful for dating the pattern's adoption curve; by 2025-26 the relationship has inverted and the untreated grey-shimmer skeleton is itself the templated/AI-default loading look the pipeline should avoid.
claims.quote: Progression bars and spinners have long been the norm when providing feedback during wait times on the web. However, a more recent trend is the use of skeleton screens.

claims.claim: Codrops' retrospective identifies 3D and WebGL — specifically Three.js and React Three Fiber — as the single dominant theme of its 2025 output, which makes WebGL-heavy creative portfolios the mainstream default of the 2025 creative-web scene rather than a differentiator. For an anti-template pipeline this is a cliché-risk signal: the 'shader-driven 3D portfolio' is now the field's most-taught form, and it also directly violates the sub-100KB shell unless deferred behind a designed no-WebGL fallback.
claims.quote: A dominant theme throughout the year was 3D and WebGL, with many tutorials centered around Three.js, React Three Fiber, and related workflows.

claims.claim: The review enumerates a concrete, closed list of the interaction patterns that recurred across 2025 creative-web work: scroll-based interactions, grids, carousels, draggable elements, custom cursors, typography experiments, infinite layouts, and marquees. This is usable directly as a saturation/cliché watchlist — these are the patterns most likely to make two independent 2025-vintage portfolio builds look alike.
claims.quote: Scroll-based interactions, grids, carousels, draggable elements, cursors, typography experiments, infinite layouts, and marquees.

claims.claim: GSAP became fully free in 2025, including its previously paid plugins SplitText and MorphSVG, removing the licensing barrier to per-character/word text splitting and SVG shape morphing. This changes the cost calculus for motion technique selection but does not change the byte cost — GSAP plus plugins is a heavy runtime that belongs in the deferred layer, not the shell.
claims.quote: GSAP becoming fully free... Opening up powerful plugins like SplitText and MorphSVG unlocked a whole new level of creative freedom.

claims.claim: WebGPU and TSL (Three.js Shader Language) are positioned by Codrops as 2025's emerging rendering frontier, alongside fluid simulation, procedural 3D generation, real-time dithering shaders and video-to-WebGL projection mapping. Every one of these is GPU-dependent and therefore requires the pipeline's mandated third tier — a designed no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback — since WebGPU support is narrower still than WebGL.
claims.quote: WebGPU (positioned as emerging frontier) ... TSL (Three.js Shader Language) ... Real-time dithering shader (Niccolò Fanton) ... Fluid simulations via WebGPU ... Video-to-WebGL projection mapping

claims.claim: This retrospective contains no discussion of homogenization, templated or AI-default aesthetics, and frames AI purely as a development tool rather than as a force acting on visual style — so it cannot be cited as evidence for the anti-generic discourse. It is evidence of what the creative-web community built in 2025, not of what that community considers generic.
claims.quote: We explored emerging topics such as AI, including tutorials on AI agents and AI-assisted development, showing how these tools can support performance monitoring, physics systems.

claims.claim: Apple's Liquid Glass is mechanically distinct from prior glassmorphism/frosted-glass: it refracts and bends background content (lensing) rather than merely scattering/blurring it, and is composed of three stacked layers — highlight (light casting and movement), shadow (depth separation), and illumination (material flexibility). This gives a falsifiable four-part spec for a STYLES.md entry that is not the existing frosted-glass vocabulary.
claims.quote: Background elements are bended and warped rather than scattering light as it's been in previous designs. There's gel-like feel to elements. ... Liquid glass is composed of layers: highlight (light casting and movement), shadow (added depth for separation between foreground and background), and illumination (the flexible properties of the material).

claims.claim: The web reproduction of Liquid Glass is CSS/SVG-native — an SVG filter (displacement) combined with backdrop-filter and nested containers approximating the three-layer model — but the SVG-filter approach does not work in Safari, so any use requires a designed non-refracting fallback. This satisfies the pipeline's 'CSS/SVG-native, cheap' preference while violating its 'must ship a fallback' rule unless the fallback is authored.
claims.quote: The most common approaches appear to reach for SVG filters and background blurs, though there are many programmatic demos as well. ... thanks for the article, but unfortunately the filter approach doesn't work in safari :(

claims.claim: Translucent UI produces variable, non-deterministic contrast ratios — text that passes WCAG over one backdrop fails over another (e.g. a bright photo) — meaning contrast cannot be statically verified for any translucent component and must be guaranteed by an opaque scrim or a contrast floor.
claims.quote: When you have translucent elements letting background colors bleed through, you're creating variable contrast ratios that might work well over one background, but fail over a bright photo of the sunset.

claims.claim: Liquid Glass's documented failure mode is loss of affordance: controls dissolve into shapes that no longer signal their mechanics, which is a component-pattern (not merely aesthetic) cost and directly relevant to the pipeline's 'Fails' field.
claims.quote: Buttons become amorphous shapes. Sliders lose their mechanical clarity. Toggle switches abandon their physical affordances.

claims.claim: Apple itself walked the effect back during the iOS 26 beta cycle by raising opacity and 'frost' for legibility, and shipped a user-facing glass transparency slider — empirical evidence from the originating vendor that the maximally transparent form is not shippable and that a user-controllable reduced variant is required.
claims.quote: Apple has already adjusted Liquid Glass between beta releases, increasing opacity and "frost" to improve legibility. iOS 27 updates include a "new glass transparency slider" for user control.

claims.claim: Apple defines Liquid Glass by a specific, nameable optical mechanic — "lensing," real-time bending/concentration of light — explicitly distinguished from the light-scattering blur materials that preceded it (iOS 7 realtime blurs, frosted glassmorphism). This gives the 2025-26 movement a falsifiable defining mechanic distinct from the glassmorphism already in circulation, and it is reproducible on the web via SVG feDisplacementMap / backdrop-filter / WebGL refraction rather than a plain backdrop blur.
claims.quote: The primary way Liquid Glass visually defines itself is through something called Lensing… Where as previous materials scattered light, this new set of materials dynamically bends, shapes, and concentrates light in real time. This provides definition against the background content while still feeling visually grounded in our experience of the natural world.

claims.claim: Apple names three explicit anti-patterns/failure modes for the style: applying it to the content layer, stacking glass on glass, and tinting every element. These are vendor-documented failure conditions, directly usable as the "Fails" clause of a style entry, and they predict the exact way the look degrades when copied at scale into templated sites.
claims.quote: always avoid glass on glass Stacking Liquid Glass elements on top of each other can quickly make the interface feel cluttered and confusing… Avoid tinting all your elements. When every element is tinted, nothing stands out, and it can be confusing… it is best reserved for the navigation layer that floats above the content of your app.

claims.claim: Apple's reduced-motion treatment of Liquid Glass is a designed degradation, not a disablement: Reduced Motion lowers effect intensity and removes elastic behaviour while the material persists, and Reduced Transparency/Increased Contrast substitute frostier fills and contrasting borders rather than removing the element. This is a first-party precedent for the pipeline's rule that every technique ships a designed reduced-motion still instead of `animation: none`.
claims.quote: Reduced Transparency, makes Liquid Glass frostier and obscures more of the content behind it. Increased contrast, makes elements predominantly black or white and highlights them with a contrasting border. Reduced Motion decreases the intensity of some effects and disables any elastic properties for the material.

claims.claim: The "Clear" (non-adaptive, permanently transparent) variant is gated behind three stated preconditions — media-rich content beneath, a content layer that tolerates a dimming layer, and bold/bright content above — and legibility is documented to fail without the dimming layer. This is a precise, checkable "Right when" condition set plus its measured failure mode, and it flags the accessibility cost of the transparent look.
claims.quote: Clear should only be used when these 3 conditions are met. First, the element you're applying it to is over media-rich content. Second, your content layer won't be negatively affected by introducing a dimming layer. And lastly, the content sitting above it is bold and bright… To provide enough legibility for symbols or labels, it needs a dimming layer to darken the underlying content. Without it, legibility gets noticeably worse.

claims.claim: Apple specifies state-change motion for the material as morphing and materialization rather than cross-fade: controls shape-shift between app sections on a single floating plane, menus pop open in place from the tapped button, and elements materialize by modulating lensing instead of fading opacity. This is a platform-HIG-level argument for shared-element/container-transform motion (View Transitions API territory) over opacity fades for drawers, menus and panels.
claims.quote: As you go between states in an app, Liquid Glass dynamically morphs between the controls in each context… Instead of fading, Liquid Glass objects materialize in and out by gradually modulating the light bending and lensing, ensuring a graceful transition that preserves the optical integrity of the material.

result.evidence:
I extracted full text from the JSTOR scan of the primary paper (Cleveland & McGill 1984, JASA 79(387):531-554) and verified every load-bearing element verbatim. Extracted text at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-taha/b7953e86-7295-434f-af62-abc041f9f51e/scratchpad/webfetch-1785152133788-ud1wvx.pdf.txt.

CONFIRMED VERBATIM:
1. The six-tier list, exactly as claimed (p.535-536): "The following are the 10 elementary tasks in Figure 1, ordered from most to least accurate: 1. Position along a common scale 2. Positions along nonaligned scales 3. Length, direction, angle 4. Area 5. Volume, curvature 6. Shading, color saturation".
2. The ties sentence (p.537): "Three of the ranks-3, 5, and 6-have more than one task; at the moment there is not enough information to separate the ties."
3. The design rule, verbatim in the abstract: "The theory provides a guideline for graph construction: Graphs should employ elementary tasks as high in the ordering as possible."
4. "HYPOTHESIZED" is the paper's own word, not the claimant's gloss (p.535): "In this section we hypothesize an ordering of the 10 elementary perceptual tasks on the basis of the accuracy with which people can extract quantitative information by using them." And on basis (p.537): "The hypothesized ordering of the elementary tasks is based on information from a variety of sources: our own reasoning and experimentation with various graph forms, results of psychophysical experiments, and the theory of psychophysics."
5. Area/volume are explicitly theoretical, not measured here (p.537-538): "length judgments are hypothesized to be more accurate than area judgments, which in turn are hypothesized to be more accurate than volume judgments. This ordering is based on a combination of psychophysical theory and experimental results" — i.e. imported prior results, no experiment in this paper.

ONE CORRECTION REQUIRED (does not overturn the claim; it errs in the paper's favour, over-crediting the experiments). The claim says "only tiers 1 vs 2 vs 3 were experimentally tested." Tier 2 was NOT tested. Section 4.2 states the position-length experiment used only "Judgment Types 1-3, subjects had to judge position along a common scale, and for Judgment Types 4 and 5, subjects had to judge length"; the second was the position-angle (bar vs pie) experiment. Section 4.1 summarises: "The experiments demonstrated very clearly that some judgments of position along a common scale are more accurate than some judgments of length and of angle." Tier 2's rank rests solely on a Weber's-Law argument about framed rectangles ("The reason for putting position along nonaligned scales ahead of length is that there are additional visual cues"). Correct wording: only tier 1 vs tier 3 (length, and separately angle) was experimentally tested; tiers 2, 4, 5, 6 are theoretical in this paper.

TWO QUALIFICATIONS TO CARRY INTO THE REPORT (neither refutes the claim): (a) the paper itself limits the rule's force — "The ordering of the perceptual tasks does not provide a complete prescription for how to make a graph. Rather, it provides a set of guidelines that must be used with judgment in designing a graph"; and the authors concede overlap — "it might be argued that judging positions along nonaligned scales really involves making two length judgments". (b) Downstream literature qualifies the ranking's generality: Heer & Bostock (CHI 2010) replicated position>length>angle on Mechanical Turk and extended it to circular/rectangular area, while McColeman et al., "The Risks of Ranking" (arXiv:2212.10533), find the encoding rankings do not hold under a different task and that factors such as cardinality outweigh encoding choice. So the ranking should be cited as a design prior, not a law.

Source quality: primary, peer-reviewed JASA paper, cited directly; claim is historical so "outdated" does not apply; no marketing content involved.
result.counterSource: McColeman et al., "The Risks of Ranking: Revisiting Graphical Perception to Model Individual Differences in Visualization Performance" (arXiv:2212.10533) — finds the Cleveland-McGill encoding rankings do not hold under a different task, and that cardinality influences performance more than encoding choice. Qualifies downstream generality only; does not contradict what the 1984 paper states. Also Heer & Bostock, CHI 2010 (crowdsourced replication, largely confirmatory).

Skau & Kosara, "Arcs, Angles, or Areas: Individual Data Encodings in Pie and Donut Charts," Computer Graphics Forum (EuroVis) 2016, doi:10.1111/cgf.12888, and Kosara, "Evidence for Area as the Primary Visual Cue in Pie Charts," IEEE VIS Short 2019 (kosara.net/papers/2019/Kosara-VISShort-2019.pdf) — these qualify the MECHANISM (angle is likely not the cue readers actually use in pie charts; area/arc dominate) but do not dispute the reported error rates. Heer & Bostock, CHI 2010, doi:10.1145/1753326.1753357, independently replicated the position>length>angle ranking on Mechanical Turk. No source found disputing the statistic.
result.evidence:
VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCE, NOT JUST THE SUPPLIED QUOTE. The linked PDF is a JSTOR image scan with no text layer (pdftotext yields only the 1,686-byte JSTOR cover page), so I rendered and read the page images directly. The passages are verbatim.

p.541, section headed "Large Absolute Errors": "The top panel of Figure 17 shows a summary of the large errors for the position-length experiment. Of the 2,550 judgments made by the subjects, 136 had a log error greater than 4."
p.542 (continuation): "Seventy-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the length judgments; since there were three position judgments for each two length judgments, the rate of occurrence of large errors for length judgments is 5.3 times that for position judgments. The bottom panel of Figure 17 shows the percentage of large errors (those greater than 4) for the position-angle experiment; in this experiment 219 of the 4,080 judgments had large errors. Eighty-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the angle judgments; thus the rate of occurrence of large errors for the angle judgments is 7.3 times that for the position judgments."

Arithmetic checks out internally: 51 usable subjects x 50 judgments = 2,550 (p.539/p.540: "In the position-length experiment there were 50 judgments"; "For both experiments, 51 subjects remained for analysis"); 51 x 80 = 4,080 (p.540: "In the position-angle experiment there were 80 judgments"). Length large-error rate = 0.78x136/1020 = 0.104 vs position 0.22x136/1530 = 0.0196 -> 5.3x. Angle = 0.88x219/2040 vs 0.12x219/2040 -> 7.33x. Both derived ratios reproduce.

The comparative framing ("stronger argument than the mean-accuracy factor alone") is also supported by the same paper: p.541 gives the position-angle mean difference as ".97 on the log scale, which is a factor of 2^.97 = 1.96" — so the tail ratio (7.3x) is materially larger than the mean ratio (1.96x), exactly as the claim asserts. Source is peer-reviewed JASA 1984, the canonical primary source; not marketing, not a listicle, not a press release. Not outdated: Heer & Bostock (CHI 2010) replicated the ranking.

QUALIFICATIONS THE PIPELINE SHOULD CARRY (do not invalidate the claim, but bound it):
1. "log error > 4" is on the paper's scale log2(|judged percent - true percent| + 1/8) (defined p.540), i.e. an absolute error of roughly >15.9 percentage points. Cite the threshold's meaning, not just the words "large error", or the number is unfalsifiable folklore downstream.
2. These are descriptive counts with no confidence intervals and are derived from rounded percentages (78%, 88%) of 136 and 219 events; the bootstrap CIs in the paper (section 4.4) apply to the mean log-error, not to the large-error ratios. Do not report 5.3x/7.3x as statistically tested effects.
3. The paper itself attributes much of the length/angle error to systematic bias, not random noise: p.544, "An important part of the contribution to the errors for length and angle judgments is consistent bias. When the true percentages are in the range of 25-50%, subjects tend to underestimate values." So "catastrophic misreading" here is partly directional underestimation, which is a slightly different design implication than random scatter.
4. The claim's phrase "pie/angle encodings" fuses a stimulus with a mechanism. Cleveland & McGill's experiment 2 stimulus was pie charts vs bar charts (p.539), and they LABELLED the pie task "angle". Skau & Kosara 2016 and Kosara 2019 argue angle is not the cue readers actually use; area is. Safer wording for STYLES.md/CRAFT.md: "the pie-chart condition (which Cleveland & McGill treated as an angle judgment)".

I OCR-read the actual JSTOR scan of Cleveland & McGill 1984 (JASA 79(387):531–554) at the cited URL. The quote is VERBATIM from pp. 541–542, section headed "Large Absolute Errors" (accompanying Figure 17, "Percentage of large errors"):

p.541: "The top panel of Figure 17 shows a summary of the large errors for the position–length experiment. Of the 2,550 judgments made by the subjects, 136 had a log error greater than 4."
p.542: "Seventy-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the length judgments; since there were three position judgments for each two length judgments, the rate of occurrence of large errors for length judgments is 5.3 times that for position judgments. ... in this experiment 219 of the 4,080 judgments had large errors. Eighty-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the angle judgments; thus the rate of occurrence of large errors for the angle judgments is 7.3 times that for the position judgments."

ARITHMETIC CROSS-CHECK against the design described on pp.539–540 — all self-consistent, which rules out a garbled or hallucinated quote:
- 51 subjects retained after exclusions (p.539); position–length = 50 judgments/subject (10 ratios x 5 types) → 51x50 = 2,550. Position–angle = 80 judgments/subject (40 ratios x 2 types) → 51x80 = 4,080. Both totals match exactly.
- Types 1–3 = position along a common scale, Types 4–5 = length (p.539), i.e. 3 position : 2 length. Recomputing: 0.78x136 = 106 length errors / 1,020 length judgments = 10.4%; 0.22x136 = 30 / 1,530 = 1.96%; ratio = 5.32 ≈ 5.3. ✓
- Position–angle is 1:1 (2,040 each): 0.88x219 = 193/2,040 = 9.45%; 0.12x219 = 26/2,040 = 1.29%; ratio = 7.33 ≈ 7.3. ✓
- Threshold decoded: error = log2(|judged% − true%| + 1/8) (p.540), so "log error > 4" = absolute error > 15.9 percentage points on a 0–100 scale. Calling that "gross failure" is fair, not inflation.

THE INTERPRETIVE STEP HOLDS TOO. The claim's comparative ("stronger than the mean-accuracy factor alone") is arithmetically true against the paper's own mean figures: angle vs position mean difference is ".97 on the log scale, which is a factor of 2^.97 = 1.96" (p.541); length vs position "40%–250% larger" (1.4x–2.5x). 5.3x and 7.3x exceed both. Critically, the paper states it used MIDMEANS "principally because of the outliers" (p.540) — so the headline mean factors deliberately trim exactly these tails, which is why the large-error rate is genuinely additional information rather than a restatement. Angle stimuli were pie charts and position stimuli bar charts (p.539), so "pie/angle" is the authors' own framing, not the claimant's invention. Blunder confounds are ruled out: "Only four errors occurred in the choice of which bar or segment was smaller" (p.539).

CAVEATS TO CARRY INTO THE REPORT (qualify, do not refute): (1) The >4 threshold is post-hoc and unpreregistered; no test statistic or CI is reported for either ratio, and judgments are clustered within 51 subjects, so these are descriptive rates, not inferential — the word "governs" is stronger than the paper's own language. (2) The paper itself hedges generalization: "Strictly speaking we cannot do more than assert that the results hold for the particular types of graphs in the experiment" (p.538). Heer & Bostock, CHI 2010 "Crowdsourcing Graphical Perception" replicated the Cleveland–McGill position/length/angle/area stimuli on Mechanical Turk and obtained results very similar to the original. The genuine critiques (McColeman, Yang, Brady, Franconeri, "Rethinking the Ranks of Visual Channels," IEEE TVCG 2021, arXiv:2107.11367; also Simkin & Hastie 1987 JASA and Spence & Lewandowsky 1991) do not dispute the 1984 measurements — they challenge the GENERALIZABILITY of the derived ranking, arguing two-value ratio judgment is a narrow proxy for real chart tasks and that some individuals credibly deviate from the canonical ordering.

1. Scope. The numbers hold for one task — "what percentage one value was of a larger value" — on specific 1984 print stimuli. The authors themselves hedge on p. 538: "Strictly speaking we cannot do more than assert that the results hold for the particular types of graphs in the experiment." Do NOT let the survey report state a universal "bars beat pies" law; part-of-whole and summation tasks are the documented exception (Spence & Lewandowsky 1991).
2. "Accuracy" here is the ratio of midmean log2 absolute-error magnitudes, not a hit rate; and 1.4–2.5 are the BOUNDS across best/worst position–length pairings, not a single uniform effect. Exp 1 used grouped and divided bar charts only — no pie charts — so "judging bar charts and pie charts" is the paper's own collective phrasing across both experiments, not per-experiment.

(2) THE QUOTED SUMMARY — CONFIRMED VERBATIM: "For all types of judgments, subjects made visual assessments of what percentage one value was of a larger value; thus all recorded values were between 0 and 100. In both experiments there were 51 subjects with usable data. ... In the first experiment, position judgments were more accurate than length judgments by factors varying from 1.4 to 2.5. In the second experiment, position judgments were 1.96 times as accurate as angle judgments."

(3) DERIVATION TRACED (p. 541), which the claim omits and the report should carry: the metric is the midmean of log base 2 of (absolute error + 0.125). "The larger of the two length values is 1.32 log units greater than the smallest of the three position values, which is a factor of 2^1.32 = 2.5. The smaller length value is .51 log units greater than the largest position value, which is a factor of 1.4." And: "The difference is .97 on the log scale, which is a factor of 2^.97 = 1.96, and is statistically significant." So "N times as accurate" = ratio of geometric-mean absolute errors, NOT an accuracy score. 95% CIs were bootstrapped.

SOURCE QUALITY: maximal for the claim's strength — peer-reviewed JASA, the foundational primary paper, authors at AT&T Bell Labs. Independently replicated by Heer & Bostock, CHI 2010 (MTurk replication), which broadly confirmed the position < length < angle error ordering. Not marketing, not a listicle, not forum speculation.

DEFECT 1 (must be corrected before use): the claim describes both experiments as "judging bar charts and pie charts." Wrong for experiment 1. The position-length experiment used bar charts only — five judgment types across grouped and divided bar charts ("which of the two bars or two segments was the smaller... judge what percentage the smaller was of the larger"). Pie charts appear ONLY in experiment 2, which paired an ordinary bar chart against a pie chart with the task "to judge what percent each of the other segments or bars is of the largest."

DEFECT 2 (over-firmness): the paper hedges the very numbers the claim presents as hard: "The means in Figure 16 provide convenient, but rough, summaries of the two experiments. The summaries are rough because it is clear from Figures 13 and 14 that there is some dependence of log error on the true percent. Within an experiment it is reasonable to compare the means of the judgments... but it would be inappropriate to compare the means of the first experiment with those of the second." So 1.4-2.5 and 1.96 must never be chained or averaged into a single cross-experiment ranking.

DEFECT 3 (scope of the trailing "i.e."): "bar chart beats pie chart by roughly a factor of 2" is accurate ONLY for experiment 2's task (judging each value as a percent of the largest value). VERDICT: the quote is real and correctly transcribed, but the claim misstates the study's design/statistics AND inverts its applicability to sparklines. Refuted on three independent grounds.

(1) INTERNAL CONTRADICTION / CONFLATED RUNS. I downloaded the primary PDF (Heer & Bostock, "Crowdsourcing Graphical Perception," CHI 2010) and extracted the text. Verbatim: "We used a 2 (chart) x 3 (height) x 4 (gridline spacing) factorial design with 3 replications, for a total of 72 trials (HITs). Either a bar chart or a line chart was shown with a height of 40, 80, or 160 pixels." 320px was NOT in that design — it came from a separate follow-up: "We subsequently conducted a second experimental run, denoted as 3B. The extended experiment used chart heights of 160 and 320 for a total of 48 HITs. We again requested N=24 assignments, but raised the reward to $0.04 per HIT." So 2x3x4 x 3 reps x N=24 = 1,728 responses, not 2,880; 2,880 = 1,728 (3A) + 1,152 (3B) pooled. A 2x3x4 design cannot yield F(3, ...) for height — df=3 requires 4 levels, i.e. the pooled 40/80/160/320. The claim staples "2x3x4 factorial" to "2,880 responses" and "F(3,2802)" as if one experiment; those three numbers cannot all belong to the same design. Worse for the specific "320 is indistinguishable" part: the same paper reports "a small but significant effect of reward on accuracy (F(1,1136) = 7.79, p < 0.005): Turkers were less accurate (delta-mu = 1.4 units) when paid more" — and 3B (the only source of the 320px condition) paid double. The 320px comparison is confounded by a documented pay-rate accuracy effect and a 3-month-later subject pool.

(2) THE 40px RESULT IS A GRIDLINE-CROWDING RESULT, NOT A SIZE FLOOR — and the paper's own stated implication is one-directional. The task was NOT sparkline reading: "Subjects were shown a chart and asked to first indicate which marked element (the left or the right) was smaller and then estimate the difference between the two... Each chart consisted of 12 values distributed on a range of 0-100 units. Each value was labeled A-L," with gridlines "drawn at intervals of 10, 20, 50, or 100 units." The height x spacing interaction was significant (F(9,2802) = 2.11, p < 0.026) and the authors attribute the small-chart error to gridline crowding: "Error increased steeply in charts with a height of 40 pixels and gridline spacing of 10 units. Presumably the dense packing of gridlines impedes accurate tracing to their labels." (10 units on 40px = 4px apart, below their own 8px rule.) The paper's Conclusion states only the ceiling, never a floor: "gridlines should be spaced at least 8 pixels apart and increasing chart heights beyond 80 pixels provides little accuracy benefit on a 0-100 scale." Sparklines by definition carry no gridlines, no axis labels, and are read for trend/shape, not labeled value tracing — so the mechanism behind the 40px penalty does not transfer.

(3) DIRECTLY CONTRADICTED BY THE CLOSEST PRIOR WORK, BY THE SAME AUTHOR, USING THE SAME ERROR METRIC. Heer, Kong & Agrawala, "Sizing the Horizon," CHI 2009 (Best Paper; controlled lab displays, sizes reported in mm) — the study Heer & Bostock cite as their inspiration [12] — measured the identical judgment (estimate the value difference between two marked points) and found the OPPOSITE practical threshold: "For all three chart types, scale factor 1/2 (24 pixels) resulted in faster but comparably accurate performance over charts twice as large" and "for both normal line charts and 1-band mirror charts, we found a chart height of 24 pixels (6.8 mm on our 14.1" 1024 x 768 pixel displays) to be optimal." Error only degrades below that: "At resolutions below 24 pixels, error appears to increase linearly as the virtual resolution halves." They further recommend 2-band charts down to "6 pixels (1.7 mm) or more." So a gridline-free micro-chart at 24px was measured as optimal, not "measurably too small" — the claim's headline design rule ("40px is measurably too small," implying ~80px minimum for sparklines) is falsified for the exact genre it is being applied to. Note also that 80px is far taller than any sparkline: Tufte's sparkline is word/line-of-text sized (~15-25px), so "shrunk to ~80px" describes no real sparkline.

ADDITIONAL WEAKNESSES: the authors themselves flag the pixel threshold as un-normalizable — "the subjects' physical display size, resolution, and viewing distance can not be measured reliably" — which is why the 2009 lab paper reports mm alongside px. A raw 2009-era pixel number is further eroded by HiDPI/devicePixelRatio and CSS-px reference scaling in 2026.

WHAT SURVIVES (the usable, defensible version): "In gridlined bar/line charts read for labeled value differences on a 0-100 scale, accuracy plateaus by ~80px height; increasing beyond 80px buys little (Heer & Bostock, CHI 2010). Gridlines must be >=8px apart; the 40px penalty appears where dense gridlines crowd below that. For gridline-free micro-charts/sparklines, the relevant measurement is Heer/Kong/Agrawala CHI 2009: ~24px is optimal for value-difference estimation, with error rising only below it." The claim as submitted should not be entered into the reference library in its current form.

Nothing sparkline-shaped was tested.

2. THE 40px PENALTY IS LARGELY A GRIDLINE ARTIFACT, NOT A SIZE EFFECT. The paper reports a significant height×spacing interaction, F(9,2802)=2.11, p<0.026, and attributes the spike explicitly: "Error increased steeply in charts with a height of 40 pixels and gridline spacing of 10 units. Presumably the dense packing of gridlines impedes accurate tracing to their labels. The results suggest that gridlines be separated by at least 8 pixels." A gridline-free sparkline at 40px has no such mechanism.

A plain line chart at 24px read as accurately as at 48px under lab control. That falsifies "40px is measurably too small" as a micro-chart rule.

4. 80px IS RANGE-DEPENDENT, NOT AN ABSOLUTE. The paper conditions it twice — "when using a 0-100 scale" and "This size roughly coincides with the point at which the pixel and data resolutions match." The claim's actionable sentence drops the condition; by the paper's own logic a 0-10 range plateaus near 10px.

Every number in the claim is real. Source quality is excellent (peer-reviewed CHI, primary). Not marketing.

1. WRONG STIMULUS CLASS — the word "sparkline" appears nowhere in the study. The stimuli were bar/line charts of "12 values distributed on a range of 0-100 units," each "labeled A-L," WITH gridlines at 10/20/50/100-unit intervals and axis labels; the task was "indicate which marked element... was smaller and then estimate the difference between the two," scored as |judged difference - true difference|. That is precise numeric value extraction from a gridded, labeled, framed chart. A sparkline (Tufte, Beautiful Evidence 2006) is by definition word-sized, frameless, gridline-less, tick-less, read for trend not for numeric difference. Generalizing this to "a sparkline can be shrunk to ~80px" inverts the genre — an 80px-tall sparkline is not a sparkline.

2. THE 80px NUMBER IS DATA-RANGE-DERIVED, NOT A SIZE CONSTANT — the paper's own explanation: "This size roughly coincides with the point at which the pixel and data resolutions match" (0-100 scale ≈ ~1px per unit). It is a resolution-matching result, not a portable "micro-charts need 80px" threshold. The claim keeps "on a 0-100 scale" in sentence one and silently drops it in the actionable sentence.

3. DIRECTLY CONTRADICTED FOR THE MICRO-CHART CASE by Heer, Kong & Agrawala, "Sizing the Horizon," CHI 2009 — the study Heer & Bostock cite as ref [12] and name as the inspiration for this very experiment. Extracted verbatim (idl.cs.washington.edu/files/2009-TimeSeries-CHI.pdf): "Estimation error remained steady for scale factors of 1 and 1/2" (= 48px and 24px); "For both normal line charts and 1-band mirror charts, we found a chart height of 24 pixels (6.8 mm on our 14.1" 1024x768 pixel displays) to be optimal. For 2-band line charts, we found optima at 12 and 6 pixels (3.4 and 1.7 mm)"; "we recommend using 2-band charts for chart heights of 6 pixels (1.7 mm) or more"; and it tested heights down to 2px. So for small time-series charts — exactly what a sparkline is — a same-lab primary study measured 24px as OPTIMAL and error stable down to 24px, flatly contradicting "40px is measurably too small."

4. THE 40px PENALTY IS PARTLY A GRIDLINE ARTIFACT — there was a significant height x spacing interaction (F(9,2802)=2.11, p<0.026) and the paper notes "Error increased steeply in charts with a height of 40 pixels and gridline spacing of 10 units. Presumably the dense packing of gridlines impedes accurate tracing to their labels. The results suggest that gridlines be separated by at least 8 pixels." Sparklines have no gridlines, so the mechanism driving the 40px penalty does not exist in the target application.

5. INTERNAL INCOHERENCE IN THE CLAIM — "3 (height)" with four heights listed and F df=3 (four levels). The paper resolves this (run 3A = 40/80/160, follow-up run 3B added 160/320); the claim compresses both runs into one design description that cannot produce df=3.

UNIT/AGE CAVEAT — 2010 CSS pixels, pre-Retina, with the authors stating physical display size, resolution and viewing distance "can not be measured reliably"; the 2009 companion states "we did not vary physical pixel sizes... left to future work." (1) "only if" is a logical strengthening the design cannot support. There was NO no-gridline control condition. The factorial was 2 (chart) x 3 (height) x 4 (gridline spacing), with spacing levels of 10, 20, 50, 100 UNITS on a 0-100 scale — never a "none" level. The paper reports a main effect plus one degraded cell, not a conditional. It never shows sub-8px gridlines are worse than no gridlines.

(2) The "8 pixels" is not a measured threshold — it is the next value tested above a single failing cell. Converting the design to pixels: the only sub-8px condition in the ENTIRE experiment is 40px height x 10 units = 4px. Every other cell is 8, 16, 32, 40, 64, 80, 160 or 320px. No 5px, 6px or 7px condition exists, so the true boundary is unresolvable between 4 and 8px. Calling this "a concrete, checkable rule" asserts precision the 4-level coarse factor cannot deliver.

(3) The stated mechanism is the authors' explicit speculation, not a finding. The paper hedges: "PRESUMABLY the dense packing of gridlines impedes accurate tracing to their labels." (4) "dense chart and TABLE design" is an unlicensed domain transfer. Stimuli were bar and line charts with 12 values, labeled A-L, comparing values D and I. Grep of the full text returns zero table stimuli. Applying an axis-gridline spacing rule to table hairline rules is nonsense in practice — 8px between row rules implies 8px rows.

The paper states "the subjects' physical display size, resolution, and viewing distance can not be measured reliably" (resolutions 1024x768 to 1920x1200, all ~1x DPI, 2009). 1) NOT A MEASUREMENT OF READERS — the central overreach. The claim says the figure shows "a reader's visual interpretation" diverging, and calls it "a measured distortion figure." No human was ever tested. Fig. 3's caption (verified via PMC7595127) defines the quantity purely colorimetrically: "The incremental lightness difference, ΔE, here using the CIEDE2000 formulation ... Using the cumulative colour lightness difference, ΔE_Cumulative, it is possible to extract the resulting visual error in percentage of total data variation ... For non-scientific colour maps, like jet, data gradients are unevenly represented and visual error can be >7% of the displayed data variation." That is a formula evaluated on the colormap's own LUT versus a linear ramp — a property of the colormap, not a behavioural measurement. Reference 30 is a self-citation to Crameri (2018), Geosci. Model Dev. 11:2541–2562, a MATLAB geodynamics-software paper, where the origin number is stated as "CIE76 lightness variations along the standard rainbow colour bar introduce a significant error of 7.5% across the colour bar range ... while the error of the perceptually uniform colour map davos is only 1.6%." Note the metric shifts from CIE76 (7.5%) to CIEDE2000 (>7%) between the two papers — sensitivity to an arbitrary ΔE formulation choice, which is not what "measured" implies.

2) HEDGE STRIPPED. Source says "CAN diverge ... by more than seven percent" and "visual error CAN BE >7%" — an illustrative ceiling for jet in one worked example. The claim converts this into a general causal effect: rainbow maps "cause a reader's visual interpretation to diverge ... by more than 7%."

3) "STRONGEST AVAILABLE ARGUMENT FOR BANNING" IS CONTRADICTED by the subsequent literature. Reda, "Rainbow Colormaps: What are they good and bad for?" IEEE TVCG 2022 (PMID 36240035): "the empirical evidence behind this argument has been mixed and, at times, even contradictory," and finds observers "are more likely to discriminate global, distributional features when viewing colorful scales that induce categorization (e.g., rainbow or diverging schemes)" — i.e. rainbow has complementary utility. Ware, Turton, Bujack, Samsel, Rogers et al., "Rainbow Colormaps Are Not All Bad," IEEE CG&A 2023 (10.1109/MCG.2023.3246111). Gołębiowska & Çöltekin, "What's wrong with the rainbow?" ISPRS J. Photogramm. Remote Sens. 194:195 (2022), reviewing 37,000+ figures across 11,808 papers, concludes conflicting human-performance findings "is most likely explained by task type." A colorimetric model number from a non-experimental piece cannot be the strongest argument when task-differentiated human-subject evidence exists and points to context-dependence rather than a ban.

4) SOURCE TYPE. PubMed (33116149) lists publication type "Review" — a guidance/advocacy piece. Its Methods section covers only colour-space definitions (CIECAM02-UCS, CIELAB UCS); there is no participant experiment. Fine as a citation for the colorimetric fact; insufficient for a claim framed as measured reader behaviour and as decisive grounds for a ban.

USABLE SALVAGE for the pipeline: "Jet/rainbow colormaps are perceptually non-uniform; the cumulative CIEDE2000 lightness profile deviates from linear by >7% of displayed data range in Crameri et al.'s worked example (CIE76: 7.5% vs 1.6% for davos), so equal data steps map to unequal perceived steps." That is defensible and citable. The behavioural framing, the word "measured," and "strongest argument for banning" are not.
