That is roughly half the claimed male figure. The 8% figure is specifically a *Northern European / Caucasian-descent* figure; the literature explicitly scopes it that way ("Red–green CVD affects up to 8% of males and 0.5% of females of Northern European descent, with lower rates reported in Asian and African populations"). African male prevalence in the meta-analysis is 2.13% (female 0.34%). So "8% of men … worldwide" is a population-specific number laundered into a global one. The claim's own word "worldwide" is the part that fails.

2) SOURCE QUALITY IS MISLABELLED. Crameri, Shephard & Heron 2020, Nat Commun 11:5444 is a **Perspective/Comment about colour maps**, not an epidemiological study. The 8%/0.5% sentence is a passing secondary restatement, not a measured result of that paper. Flagging it "(primary)" is wrong — it is a secondary citation of the older Caucasian-population literature, and a 2025 meta-analysis with 1.7M participants outranks it for this specific number.

3) THE CONSEQUENT IS AN OVERREACH NOT IN THE QUOTE. The quote says only that some percentage of people have CVD. It says nothing about red-vs-green at equal lightness being "unreadable," nor about "a large fraction of readers." Severity distribution undercuts "unreadable": of the ~8% (Caucasian male) figure, roughly 1% deuteranopes + 1% protanopes are **dichromats**; ~5% deuteranomalous + ~1% protanomalous are **anomalous trichromats**, about half of whom are mild (Colour Blind Awareness; NCBI Bookshelf NBK217820, "Procedures for Testing Color Vision"). Mild deuteranomalous readers discriminate red from green with reduced, not absent, discrimination. So "unreadable" applies cleanly to ~2% of men, not 8%. And 8% of men in a mixed-sex readership is ~4.25% of readers (~2.5% using the meta-analysis figure) — calling that "a large fraction" is rhetoric, not a supported quantity.

WHAT SURVIVES (for the parent's use, but not from this source): the *design recommendation* is independently mandatory via **W3C WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.1 "Use of Color" (Level A)** — colour must not be the sole visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element. That is a genuine normative requirement and does not depend on the disputed prevalence number. A corrected, defensible version of the claim: "CVD affects ~4.4% of men and ~0.6% of women globally (Ophthalmology 2025 meta-analysis; up to 8% of men of Northern European descent), and severe red–green confusion (dichromacy) affects ~2% of men. WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 (Level A) independently requires redundant non-colour encoding regardless of prevalence." The pipeline should cite WCAG 1.4.1 as the requirement and the 2025 meta-analysis for prevalence — not the Nature Communications perspective piece.

result.evidence:
Refuted on three independent grounds.

(1) OVERREACH ON THE QUOTE. The source sentence is "Such a colour-introduced blind interpretation CAN diverge from an objective representation by MORE THAN seven percent of the displayed data variation" — a conditional upper bound for a worst case, not a general causal effect size. The claim rewrites "can diverge" as "cause a reader's visual interpretation to diverge... by more than 7%", i.e. converts a possibility ceiling into a typical measured outcome. The cited origin (ref 30 = Crameri, "Geodynamic diagnostics, scientific visualisation and StagLab 3.0", Geosci. Model Dev. 11, 2541–2562, 2018) states it as a rainbow map introducing "a visual error to the underlying data of UP TO 7.5%" — explicitly a maximum.

(2) "MEASURED, NOT FOLKLORE" IS FALSE. Crameri, Shephard & Heron 2020 (Nat Commun 11:5444) is a comment/perspective piece and reports NO human-subject experiment of its own. The 7% is analytically computed from the colour map's own lightness/perceptual profile using colour-difference metrics (ΔE CIEDE2000-type), self-cited to the author's own software-description paper (StagLab 3.0, GMD 2018), whose derivation the Nature Communications text does not reproduce. It is a property of the colour map under an assumed reading model — not a psychophysical measurement of any reader's interpretation. Attributing it to "a reader's visual interpretation" claims empirical human data that was never collected. It is model-derived, which is a category between "measured" and "folklore", and the claim asserts the wrong one.

(3) "STRONGEST AVAILABLE ARGUMENT FOR BANNING RAINBOW SCALES" IS CONTRADICTED BY LATER PEER-REVIEWED WORK. Reda, "Rainbow Colormaps: What are they good and bad for?", IEEE TVCG (IEEE VIS 2023, PMID 36240035): "Guidelines for color use in quantitative visualizations have strongly discouraged the use of rainbow colormaps... however, the empirical evidence behind this argument has been mixed and, at times, even contradictory." Its crowdsourced experiments find observers are MORE likely to discriminate global, distributional features with rainbow/categorising scales, and concludes their "complementary utility for analyzing scalar data should not be dismissed". Ware, Turton, Samsel, Bujack & Rogers, "Rainbow Colormaps Are Not All Bad", IEEE Computer Graphics & Applications 2023, argues the same against blanket dismissal. Kovesi/ISPRS-journal review "What's wrong with the rainbow? An interdisciplinary review of empirical evidence FOR AND AGAINST the rainbow color scheme" (ISPRS J. Photogramm. Remote Sens. 194, 2022) frames the evidence as two-sided. A computed 7% ceiling is strictly weaker evidence than actual human-performance studies (e.g. Borkin et al., IEEE TVCG 2011, diagnostic-accuracy differences on artery visualisation), so the claim's superlative fails even among pro-ban arguments.

USABLE RESIDUE (for the pipeline): the underlying guidance — prefer perceptually uniform / OKLCH-derived sequential and diverging scales — remains well supported. But the "7%" must be cited as "up to ~7.5% computed visual error under a perceptual-uniformity model (Crameri 2018/2020)", never as a measured reader-interpretation error, and must not be used to justify an absolute ban given Reda 2023 and Ware et al. 2023.

result.evidence:
OVERREACH ON FOUR COUNTS; the narrow reading of the quote is fine, the claim as written is not.

1. The quote says "even, MONOTONIC" — the claim drops "even" and then attributes perceptual uniformity to monotonicity alone. These are two properties. A lightness ramp can be monotonic (order preserved, greyscale-readable) yet grossly uneven (L* 20→22→24→90), which destroys perceptual uniformity — that is exactly the defect Crameri et al. attack in jet/rainbow. Saying monotonicity is "the single property that makes a scale ... perceptually uniform" misreads a conjunction as a single cause.

2. The same paper explicitly denies single-property framing. Crameri, Shephard & Heron 2020 (Nat Commun 11:5444) state: "Perceptual uniformity is a crucial property for colour maps used in science, but by no means the only property to care about. Perceptual colour order is another important aspect." They also require BRIGHTNESS, not just lightness: "To achieve perceptual order, both lightness and brightness should increase linearly" — note "linearly", stronger than "monotonic" — plus colour-vision-deficiency friendliness as a separate criterion. Lightness/brightness diverge because CIELAB L* ignores the Helmholtz–Kohlrausch effect (saturated colours look brighter than their L* implies; see Seong et al., Color Res Appl 2025, CIECAM16 lightness model incorporating H–K), so "lightness is THE load-bearing channel" is not even the source's own position.

3. The claim is stated over "a colour scale" generally and is false for two of the three families. Diverging maps are by construction NON-monotonic in lightness — Matplotlib's colormap documentation states the design goal is "monotonically increasing L* values up to a maximum, followed by monotonically decreasing L* values, with approximately equal minimum L* values at opposite ends", which means the two arms collapse onto the same greys under desaturation and the scale demonstrably does NOT survive greyscale conversion. Categorical scales likewise must not have a monotonic lightness ramp (it fabricates order). So the property is neither necessary nor sufficient in general; it is a sequential-map rule.

4. "Lightness, not hue, is the load-bearing channel" is contradicted by the foundational primary source. Ware 1988, "Color sequences for univariate maps: theory, experiments and principles" (IEEE CG&A 8(5):41–49), found the opposite tradeoff experimentally: a grey scale (pure lightness) is POOR at conveying metric/value information because of simultaneous-contrast errors, and good for form; spectrum-like hue sequences are good for value, poor for form. His conclusion is that you need lightness AND hue/saturation varying together — not lightness alone carrying the load.

5. The "directly testable by desaturating" operationalisation is unsound as stated, and the source itself hedges it: "assuming no complicated grey-scale filter is used." Desaturation is not luminance conversion. HSL desaturation maps #f00 and #0f0 both to #808080 (both are HSL L=50%), while Rec.709 luma maps them to ~54 and ~182 — a 3.4x difference. So "desaturate the chart" gives a different answer depending on whether the tool does HSL desaturation, gamma-encoded BT.601 luma, linear-light Y, or CIE L*. Only the last is the paper's lightness. The test is a useful smoke check, not the "direct" test the claim asserts.

Source quality is high (peer-reviewed Nature Communications, primary); the failure is that the claim is stronger than what its own source says, and the source contradicts it on point 2.

Its abstract does say "more than 600 million individuals worldwide with CVD" — but that sentence carries NO citation, while the 8%/0.5% sentence in the body cites refs [7] Birch 2012 and [8] Sharpe et al. 1999. Colour Blind Awareness, the most-cited advocacy source, puts the global total at ~300 million. So the claim's headline number is an uncited figure in a methods paper that contradicts both the paper's own stated prevalence and the standard estimate by roughly a factor of two.

(3) THE ETHNIC QUALIFIER IS STRIPPED, AND IT IS THE WHOLE BALL GAME FOR A ">4% OVERALL" CLAIM. The 8% figure is specific to populations of Northern European descent. Birch J. (2012), "Worldwide prevalence of red-green color deficiency," J Opt Soc Am A 29(3):313-320 — the source's OWN reference [7] — reports ~8% in European Caucasian males but 4-6.5% in Chinese/Japanese males and ~4-5% in men of African or Asian ancestry. A 2025 review (Healthcare 2025, PMC12385717) tabulates 4.0-6.9% Chinese males, ~4.0% Japanese males, 4.7% Nigerian (Imo State) males, and 2.2% South African (Durban) males, stating plainly that "red-green CVD is most common among individuals of European descent, while lower rates are reported in Asian and African populations." Weighting by world male population gives global male prevalence closer to ~5% and an overall population figure of ~2.5-3% — i.e. the claim's ">4% of the population overall" is a Britain/France-specific number (UK ~4.5%, France 8.6% male + 0.5% female = 4.5%) misapplied globally.

(4) SOURCE-STRENGTH MISMATCH. The claim labels this source "(primary)". It is not primary for prevalence — it is a 2018 colormap-design methods paper whose one-line prevalence statement is a secondary citation of Birch 2012 and a 1999 book chapter. For an epidemiological number, the primary source is Birch 2012, and Birch does not support "8% of men" as a worldwide figure.

WHAT SURVIVES: the narrow statement "~8% of men and ~0.5% of women of Northern European descent have red-green CVD; globally the figure is lower and varies by ancestry (roughly 2-7% of men)" is well supported, current, and adequate to justify CVD-safe palettes and non-color redundant encoding. The design conclusion is sound; the claim as written is not, because it inflates the worldwide headcount ~2x, universalizes a European-ancestry rate, and mislabels a methods paper as primary epidemiology. A pipeline reference library that ships "~600 million / >4%" would be propagating an uncited number the cited literature contradicts.

SOURCE AND QUOTE ARE GENUINE — the failure is overreach, on four counts.

1) "SINGLE PROPERTY" IS A COMPRESSION OF TWO, AND DROPS THE PAPER'S OWN CAVEAT. Evenness (uniform ΔL* steps) is a separate property from monotonicity; a scale can be monotonic in L* and still perceptually non-uniform. The claim's operational test — "directly testable by desaturating any generated chart" — deletes the filter caveat, and the caveat is load-bearing in a browser: CSS `filter: grayscale(1)` / feColorMatrix uses Rec.709 luma on non-linear sRGB, HSL desaturation uses (max+min)/2, and neither equals CIE L*. Different desaturation methods give different verdicts on the same palette.

2) CAUSAL MISREAD OF THE PARENTHETICAL. The quote says the palette "remains readable (as well as perceptually uniform and ordered) even after a conversion to grey scale" — i.e. these properties SURVIVE the conversion. The claim rewrites this as monotonic lightness being what MAKES a scale perceptually uniform. It does not. Perceptual uniformity is uniform perceptual arc length in a uniform space (viridis is defined by equal steps in CAM02-UCS, not by lightness alone).

3) FALSE AS A UNIVERSAL — DIVERGING AND CATEGORICAL SCALES. The pipeline's stated need covers "sequential, diverging and categorical" scales. Diverging maps are BY DESIGN non-monotonic in lightness (symmetric V-profile); Crameri's own vik/roma/berlin/managua/vanimo have minimum-or-maximum lightness at the centre and equal lightness at both ends. Kovesi (arXiv:1509.03700): "Structures in the data with values that straddle the central reference point... will be represented by colours that are effectively isoluminant, for example, blues and reds of nearly equivalent lightness. Thus, structures in this data range will be hard to resolve." Under the claim's greyscale test every diverging map fails — yet they are the correct encoding for signed deviation. Categorical palettes have no lightness order at all and hue IS the encoding. So "lightness, not hue, is the load-bearing channel" is true for exactly one of the three scale families the pipeline needs.

4) DIRECTLY CONTRADICTED BY PEER-REVIEWED EMPIRICAL WORK ON THE HUE CLAIM. Liu & Heer, CHI 2018, tested 9 colormaps: "Single-hue colormaps perform well for larger data spans... but exhibit issues of insufficient resolution at smaller spans. These results suggest that, by ramping in BOTH luminance and hue, multi-hue colormaps can provide improved discrimination WHILE PRESERVING PERCEPTION OF ORDER." Hue is therefore load-bearing for discrimination resolution, not decorative. Same paper kills the "perceptually uniform" half empirically: greys (a pure monotonic-lightness ramp) "degenerates in low luminance regions" and "the low luminance level appears to afford much worse color discrimination than that predicted by either the LAB or UCS perceptual models." A monotonic-lightness scale measurably fails perceptual uniformity in situ. Ware (1988) established the underlying tradeoff decades earlier: luminance carries FORM, hue carries METRIC/value reading — two channels, two jobs.

WHAT SURVIVES (usable narrow version): for SEQUENTIAL scales, an even monotonic L* ramp is a necessary-not-sufficient condition, and greyscale conversion via a luminance-correct filter is a cheap smoke test for ordering and CVD-safety. Anything stronger — "single property", "makes it perceptually uniform", "lightness not hue", "any generated chart" — is unsupported by the quote and contradicted by CHI 2018 and Kovesi. As written the claim would lead the pipeline to reject correct diverging and categorical palettes and to ship low-lightness ramps that test clean but read badly.

SOURCE IS REAL AND AUTHORITATIVE — the refutation is about overreach, not provenance. Crameri, Shephard & Heron, "The misuse of colour in science communication", Nat Commun 11:5444 (2020), PMC7595127, verified verbatim: "With an even, monotonic lightness gradient, a colour palette remains readable (as well as perceptually uniform and ordered) even after a conversion to grey scale, assuming no complicated grey-scale filter is used." The claim misreads this in four separable ways.

(1) DROPS "EVEN", THEN CREDITS THE RESULT TO MONOTONICITY ALONE. The source's antecedent is "even, monotonic". Evenness (uniform ΔL* increments) is what delivers perceptual uniformity; monotonicity alone delivers only ordering. Counterexample: L* = 0, 4, 8, 92, 96, 100 is strictly monotonic, survives greyscale, and is grossly non-uniform. So monotonicity is not sufficient for "remaining perceptually uniform", which is exactly what the claim asserts. The same paper separately requires "both lightness and brightness should increase linearly", i.e. linearity is a distinct requirement from monotonicity.

(2) "THE SINGLE PROPERTY" IS CONTRADICTED BY PEER-REVIEWED WORK THAT DECOMPOSES THIS INTO FOUR INDEPENDENT CRITERIA. Bujack, Turton, Samsel, Ware, Rogers & Ahrens, "The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly: A Theoretical Framework for the Assessment of Continuous Colormaps", IEEE TVCG 2018 (ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8017653) gives unambiguous separate mathematical definitions for uniformity, order, discriminative power and smoothness in CIELAB-76/CIEDE2000/CIECAM02, precisely because these terms had been conflated. Monotonic lightness supplies order; it does not supply uniformity, discriminative power (a scale monotonic over L* 45→55 is ordered, greyscale-safe, and unreadable — lightness RANGE is a second load-bearing property the claim omits), or smoothness. Kovesi, "Good Colour Maps: How to Design Them" (arXiv:1509.03700), the strongest pro-lightness source available, states the criterion as "the magnitude of the incremental change in perceptual lightness of the colours is uniform" — uniform |ΔL*|, not monotonic L* — and adds the qualification that "CIELAB space is only designed to be perceptually uniform at very low spatial frequencies", so a lightness-only test does not certify uniformity at chart-relevant spatial frequencies at all.

(3) OVER-GENERALISED FROM SEQUENTIAL TO "ANY COLOUR SCALE" — FALSIFIED BY THE SOURCE AUTHOR'S OWN PALETTES. The research question explicitly asks about sequential, DIVERGING and CATEGORICAL construction. Diverging maps are non-monotonic in lightness by construction (light centre / dark ends, or Crameri's dark-centre berlin, managua, vanimo), yet Crameri ships them as perceptually uniform. Matplotlib's "Choosing Colormaps" (matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/colors/colormaps.html) states the consequence directly: for diverging maps "if a colormap like this was used in a plot and then the plot was printed to grayscale, a lot of the information may map to the same gray values" — the two arms collapse and the SIGN of the deviation is destroyed. Cyclic maps (romaO, corkO; Kovesi's C-series) are likewise perceptually uniform with deliberately non-monotonic lightness. Both are direct counterexamples to "monotonic lightness is the single property that makes a scale perceptually uniform", and to the desaturation test as a pass/fail gate: applied blindly it would fail every valid diverging and cyclic palette. For categorical palettes (Okabe–Ito, Paul Tol) greyscale survivability requires DISTINCT lightness values, not monotonic ones — the claimed mechanism is the wrong one.

(4) THE STATED TEST IS NOT THE STATED PROPERTY, AND DROPS THE SOURCE'S OWN CAVEAT. The source hedges "assuming no complicated grey-scale filter is used"; the claim promotes this to "directly testable by desaturating any generated chart". Desaturation and greyscale conversion are not interchangeable: HSL/HSV desaturation ((max+min)/2) discards luminance entirely, while CSS `filter: grayscale(1)` / SVG `feColorMatrix type="saturate" values="0"` apply Rec.709 luma coefficients to GAMMA-ENCODED sRGB, producing luma, not the linear-light luminance Y that L* is a monotone function of (Poynton's standard luma-vs-luminance distinction). Across hues, monotone L* therefore does not guarantee monotone rendered grey — the browser test is an approximation, not a proof, which is the opposite of "directly testable".

SALVAGEABLE NARROWER FORM (what should go in the repo instead): "For SEQUENTIAL scales, an even (near-linear) monotonic L* ramp with adequate lightness range is the dominant requirement for order and greyscale survivability; `filter: grayscale(1)` is a useful smoke test, not a proof, and it does not apply to diverging, cyclic or categorical palettes." That version is supported. The claim as written is not: it collapses "even + monotonic + adequate range" into "monotonic", asserts exclusivity ("the single property") against a peer-reviewed four-criterion decomposition, and generalises a sequential-map property to all colour scales.

Not outdated (2020 source, 2018 framework, both current standards) and not marketing — refuted purely as unsupported-by-quote overreach.

2) ">4% OVERALL" IS DIRECTLY CONTRADICTED BY A 2025 META-ANALYSIS. "Global Prevalence of Congenital Color Vision Deficiency among Children and Adolescents, 1932-2022," Ophthalmology, Aug 2025 (PMID 40769301; 1,703,619 participants, 56 studies, 21 countries, 5 continents) reports pooled global prevalence 2.59% (95% CI 2.20-3.03), males 4.38%, females 0.64% (95% CI 0.46-0.89). The claim's ">4% overall" sits outside the upper bound of the 95% CI (3.03) — it is not merely imprecise, it is excluded by the interval. Same study: European descent 2.77%, African descent 2.69% — i.e. even the highest-prevalence ancestry group is nowhere near 8% overall.

3) "~600 MILLION" FAILS ON THE CLAIM'S OWN ARITHMETIC. At the claim's own generous 8%/0.5% and world population ~8.2B split evenly: (4.1B x 0.08) + (4.1B x 0.005) ≈ 328M-344M, not 600M. Using the meta-analytic 2.59%: ≈ 212M. To reach 600M you would need ~7.3% of the entire world population, which no source claims. The standard advocacy headcount (Colour Blind Awareness) is "about 300 million people worldwide" — the claim roughly doubles it. 600M appears to be folklore/inflation with no traceable source.

4) SOURCE-STRENGTH MISMATCH. The claim is labelled "(primary)" but for this specific assertion the PLOS paper is tertiary — a background sentence citing a 2012 review, which itself is superseded for global-rate purposes by the 2025 pooled analysis. A 2018 secondary restatement of a 2012 review cannot carry a 2026 quantitative claim about global population share when a 2025 systematic review with n=1.7M exists and disagrees.

Immediately after the quoted sentence: "While its CVD-simulated counterpart is CLOSE TO OPTIMAL, cmaputil helped to further improve upon this by forcing the perceptual delta to be as close to flat as possible and by increasing the light range covered." And in Future Work: "Viridis is already close to accomplishing this since the perceptual delta of the colormap, AS PERCEIVED BY SOMEONE WITH COMPLETE RED-GREEN COLORBLINDNESS, has only a SMALL IMPERFECTION toward the center." That is the paper certifying viridis as CVD-readable, just not perceptually-uniform-under-CVD. The claim converts "not CVD-OPTIMAL" into "not CVD-SAFE" — a category error. Viridis was explicitly designed for CVD in the first place (van der Walt & Smith; the R package is literally titled "Colorblind-Friendly Color Maps for R", CRAN vignette: designed "to be perceived by viewers with common forms of colour blindness", i.e. moderate deuteranomaly).

3. Independent corroboration of the refutation: Matthew Petroff, "Discernibility of (Rainbow) Colormaps" (2019): "The discernibility of Cividis, which was optimized with color vision deficiencies in mind, is the most consistent between normal color vision and various color vision deficiencies, ALTHOUGH VIRIDIS IS ALSO OKAY IN THIS REGARD, and both are considerably better than any of the rainbow colormaps."

Viridis measures as CVD-okay; cividis is more consistent, not a safety fix.

2. THE DESIGNERS' OWN PRIMARY DOCS — the viridis package (van der Walt/Smith maps, sjmgarnier port) is titled "Colorblind-Friendly Color Maps"; the CRAN vignette states the maps are "easier to read by those with colorblindness" and "print well in gray scale." Viridis's monotonic luminance ramp preserves order for dichromats by construction. A design-vocabulary entry asserting viridis is "NOT for CVD" would directly contradict the map's own authoritative documentation.

3. LATER, BROADER PEER-REVIEWED SOURCE — Crameri, Shephard & Heron 2020, Nature Communications, "The misuse of colour in science communication" (PMC7595127) treats the MPL maps ("viridis, magma, plasma and inferno") as scientifically sound perceptually-uniform maps that "spearheaded the way towards more scientific colour mapping," and positions cividis as the map that "aims to represent an almost identical appearance for red–green colour-vision deficiencies, the closest of all currently available colour maps" — i.e. cividis is best-in-class on identical-appearance, not a rescue of an unsafe viridis.

SOURCE-INDEPENDENCE PROBLEM: the sole support is the paper PROPOSING cividis. A replacement paper's characterization of the incumbent is its motivating framing, not a neutral assessment — exactly the case where a second, disinterested source is required, and the disinterested sources (1)-(3) qualify it heavily.

OVER-GENERALIZATION: "cividis is the CVD-optimized replacement" is scoped wrong. Cividis was optimized for red–green (deutan/protan) deficiency and is a blue→yellow ramp, which is the worst axis for tritanopia/tritanomaly; it also loses hue range (documented downside: "minimal coverage of different colors: varying straight from blue to yellow rather than cycling through other colors"), so it is not a general CVD upgrade. The claim only hedges this in half a sentence while the headline reads as general.

The defensible, non-refuted version is narrower: "viridis is CVD-readable (monotonic luminance, measured as okay under CVD simulation) but not CVD-optimized; cividis additionally makes red–green-CVD and non-CVD viewers see near-identical appearance. CHECK 1 — quote actually supports the claim, including the "without CVD" half. The obvious refutation path was that panels (b) and (c) are both CVD simulations, which would make "misleads WITHOUT CVD" an overreach. It is not. I pulled the verbatim Fig 1 caption from the PMC copy (PMC6070163, Nuñez/Anderton/Renslow, PLOS ONE 13(7):e0199239, 2018): "Colormaps are as follows: (a) perceptually uniform grayscale, (b) jet, (c) jet as it appears to someone with red-green colorblindness, and (d) viridis." Panel (b) is jet at normal vision. So "the bright yellow spots in (b) and (c) ... appear to represent significantly higher values than the surrounding regions. However, in fact, the dark red (in b) ... actually represent the highest values" is a normal-vision misread plus a CVD misread. The paper's body states it directly: "This can cause misinterpretation for certain types of data, even for those with normal color vision." Claim is not an overreach of the quote.

CHECK 2 — searched for contradicting evidence; the best counter concedes the mechanism. Ware, Stone & Szafir, "Rainbow Colormaps Are Not All Bad," IEEE CG&A 43(3):88-93, 2023 (doi 10.1109/MCG.2023.3246111) is the field's leading pushback and is written by three authors who had each previously argued against rainbows. It does NOT dispute the false-feature mechanism — it enumerates it as one of the three real critiques: rainbows "are not monotonic in luminance, which can distort the shapes people infer from the data" and "partition the data into distinctly colored regions or bands, which can create false divisions within the data." Their argument is mitigability ("thoughtful rainbow colormap design ... may reduce these limitations"), and they cite Turbo as the fix precisely because it "removes banding and false boundaries caused by rapid hue changes in the traditional rainbow colormap" — which presupposes that traditional jet has them. A qualification of blanket rainbow-avoidance, not a refutation of jet's failure mode.

CHECK 3 — source quality is adequate and independently corroborated. Corroboration beyond the cited primary: (a) Borland & Taylor, "Rainbow Color Map (Still) Considered Harmful," IEEE CG&A 2007 — rainbow "obscures data through its uncontrolled luminance variation" and "actively misleads interpretation through the introduction of non-data-dependent gradients"; bright stripes falsely suggest segmented regions with no basis in the data. (b) Liu & Heer, "Somewhere Over the Rainbow," CHI 2018 (idl.cs.washington.edu/files/2018-QuantitativeColor-CHI.pdf) — I extracted the PDF text; their controlled study concludes verbatim: "we confirmed that a rainbow colormap (jet) does indeed perform the worst overall in terms of both time and error, and should be jettisoned," and identifies the mechanism as name-banding that "may hamper perception if dischordant with the true value difference." Participants were general crowdworkers, i.e. predominantly non-CVD. (c) Stoelzle & Stein, HESS 25:4549, 2021, peer-reviewed, same conclusion for hydrology.

CHECK 4 — not outdated. 2018 primary, 2023 is the most recent significant discourse and it concedes the point; Google's Turbo (2019) exists specifically to repair this defect.

CHECK 5 — not marketing, not a listicle, not forum speculation. Peer-reviewed PLOS ONE + IEEE CG&A + ACM CHI.

TWO CAVEATS the report should carry, neither refuting: (i) the PLOS ONE Fig 1 normal-vision demonstration is a qualitative illustration inside a CVD-optimization paper, not a measured perceptual experiment — the measured backing is Liu & Heer 2018, whose task was relative-similarity judgment on color triplets, and who themselves caveat that "dedicated experiments in scalar field contexts might uncover additional effects." So attribute the mechanism to Borland & Taylor 2007 and the error/time penalty to Liu & Heer 2018, not both to the PLOS paper. (ii) Do not write the finding as "rainbow is always bad" — Ware/Stone/Szafir 2023 document underappreciated rainbow advantages (small-feature detection, value reading) and note avoidance has become "dogma." The defensible STYLES/CRAFT rule is narrow: jet specifically, with its non-monotonic luminance, is a documented failure mode; use OKLCH/perceptually-uniform sequential ramps (viridis/cividis class) by default.

Understanding 2.1.2 (w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/no-keyboard-trap.html, "Updated 18 May 2026"): "there may be times when it's appropriate for a web page to restrict focus to a subsection of the content – for example, when the user is inside a modal dialog or popover. The claim inverts a permission into a mandate and attaches "normative" to a non-normative guide.

REFUTATION 2 — "neither key may move focus outside the dialog" is contradicted by the currently recommended web-native implementation.
Scott O'Hara (ARIA WG participant, HTML-AAM editor), scottohara.me/blog/2019/03/05/open-dialog.html: "unlike many custom modal dialogs which typically create a focus trap – forcing an endless loop of the focusable elements within the dialog – a native modal <dialog> allows keyboard focus to escape the modal and return to the browser's chrome (e.g., the address bar and other such controls). This is good behavior, not a bug. Completely trapping keyboard focus within a custom dialog, thus not allowing focus to return to the browser chrome, was always more of a 'it's either this, or focus can move back to the document'. If this behavior seems confusing or undesired to you, that's unfortunately due to the fact that you've had to experience custom dialog behavior for so long."
So <dialog>.showModal() + inert — the 2025/26 default for drawers, sheets and bottom sheets — deliberately fails the claim's cyclic contract as literally written, and an authoritative source calls that a feature. APG's containment statement is scoped to the document's focus order; the claim promotes it to an absolute.

REFUTATION 3 — wrong mechanism named as the requirement. APG states the actual requirement is background inertness ("Windows under a modal dialog are inert") and warns "mark a dialog modal only when both" conditions hold. Containment is a consequence of inert/top-layer, not an author-written wrap loop. Prescribing the JS cycle as the contract is prescribing the legacy polyfill.

USABLE RESTATEMENT for the pipeline (what survives): a modal drawer/sheet must make the background inert (native <dialog>.showModal() or the inert attribute), move focus in on open, restore it to the invoker on close, and close on Escape (WCAG 2.1.2's "standard exit method"). Tab containment within the document follows from inertness; letting Tab reach browser chrome is correct, not a defect. A hand-rolled cyclic focus trap is a fallback for non-native implementations, not a normative requirement.

result.evidence:
Verified against the primary source itself (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/cards-component/, Page Laubheimer, NN/g, published 2016-11-06, no revision date). Every load-bearing element of the claim appears verbatim in the article, and the supporting quote given is not even the strongest one:

1. Comparison task + eyetracking + re-visiting: "Cards are also a poor choice when users need to compare between multiple options, since cards often aren't structured in a predictable way from item to item; our eyetracking research revealed that users look back and forth multiple times between items when they compare them." This is a direct, unhedged statement of the exact failure mode claimed.
2. No encoded order / semirandom scan: "The flexible-card layout does not clearly indicate a hierarchy of stories in order, so the user looks around back and forth in a semirandom pattern, looking for any compelling information." Accompanied by an actual eyetracking gaze plot ("A gaze plot of a user's eyetracking session on a card-based layout"), plus "Card layouts typically deemphasize the ranking of content."
3. Relative to consistently-positioned list rows: "A vertical list easily supports scanning for price from one product to the next, as this information is placed in a predictable location on each item in the list" and "The irregular layout makes this comparison behavior a more difficult undertaking than a vertical list."

Adversarial checks that did NOT kill it: source is primary and is explicitly one of the authority classes the research brief names (NN/g); the claim's strength ("documented failure mode") matches what a practitioner-research org can support; no marketing/press-release character; the finding is about visual search under inconsistent element positioning, which is not a fast-moving area — a 2016 date does not obsolete it, and nothing in the article has been retracted or superseded that I could locate.

Two caveats worth carrying into the report, neither sufficient to refute:
(a) "raising cognitive load" is the claim-writer's gloss, not NN/g's words. The article never uses "cognitive load," "interaction cost," or "effort"; its actual wording is "a more difficult undertaking than a vertical list." The mechanism claim should be softened to "slower / more difficult scanning" unless a separate cited source is used for the cognitive-load framing.
(b) The eyetracking is unpublished in-house NN/g research: no sample size, no methodology, no linked study, and the gaze plot shown is a single user ("a user's eyetracking session"). It is qualitative evidence from a credible practitioner lab, not a peer-reviewed measured effect — flag it as such rather than citing it as a quantified finding. The claim also slightly conflates two passages (the semirandom scan is illustrated on a news-story hierarchy; the back-and-forth revisiting is the comparison-task finding), though both are in the same article and share the stated cause (unpredictable item structure).

Limitation on my own verification: the session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted, so I could not run an independent search for contradicting literature; the verdict rests on direct source inspection, which confirmed rather than undercut the claim.

The claim's directional gist is real but its stated strength is not supported by the cited source. Verified the NN/g article (Page Laubheimer, "Cards: UI-Component Definition", published 2016-11-06) twice via independent fetch paths; both returned the same text.

WHAT THE SOURCE ACTUALLY SUPPORTS: "Cards are also a poor choice when users need to compare between multiple options, since cards often aren't structured in a predictable way from item to item; our eyetracking research revealed that users look back and forth multiple times between items when they compare them." And the caption's closing line: "The irregular layout makes this comparison behavior a more difficult undertaking than a vertical list, in which similar information would be located in predictable, consistent places for each item." Also supported: "Card layouts are less scannable than lists."

THREE SPECIFIC OVERREACHES:

1. "raising cognitive load" is NOT in the source. The article never uses "cognitive load" or any equivalent, and reports no cognitive-load measurement — no NASA-TLX, no task time, no error rate, no N. The source's actual wording is the qualitative "a more difficult undertaking." Gaze revisits are not a measure of cognitive load; NN/g does not make that inference, the claim adds it.

2. "eyetracking shows users scan in a semirandom pattern" generalizes an n=1 illustration. The word "semirandom" appears ONLY in the caption of a single gazeplot image, whose own first sentence is "A gaze plot of A USER's eyetracking session on a card-based layout" — singular, and referred to throughout as "the user"/"her". It is an illustrative single-session gazeplot, not a study with participants. The plural finding NN/g does attribute to "our eyetracking research" is only the generic "users look back and forth multiple times between items when they compare them" — which is a general statement about comparison behavior in any layout (used as an argument FOR consistent visual treatment), not a card-specific finding.

3. The gazeplot was not a comparison task. Its caption states the participant "was asked to find and read a story that looked interesting to her" — open-ended browsing/exploration. The claim recruits it as evidence about "comparison tasks." The "comparing between options" reading is the author's interpretation of one scanpath, not the assigned task.

SOURCE QUALITY / RECENCY: NN/g is an appropriate primary practitioner source for the weak form of the claim, but the article is ~10 years old (Nov 2016), links no underlying study report, gives no N, and publishes no data — insufficient for a claim worded as measured eyetracking evidence of increased cognitive load.

PROCEDURAL CAVEAT: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200), so no independent search for contradicting or qualifying evidence could be run. Per the "default to refuted if uncertain" rule that alone bars a refuted=false verdict.

A rewritten claim WOULD pass, e.g.: "NN/g reports that cards are a poor choice when users must compare options, because irregular card layouts place comparable information in unpredictable positions; an illustrative gazeplot shows a user scanning back and forth in a semirandom pattern. This is qualitative practitioner guidance (2016), not a measured cognitive-load result." Recommend the library store that version, flagged as practitioner guidance rather than measurement.

result.evidence:
VERBATIM CHECK (raw HTML pulled via curl, stripped to text — not trusting the fetch summarizer). Article: "Cards: UI-Component Definition", Page Laubheimer, NN/g. JSON-LD: datePublished 2016-11-06, dateModified 2024-02-01 (still maintained).

Every element of the claim maps to verbatim source text, and the article says MORE than the supplied supporting quote:

1. "failure mode for comparison tasks" — verbatim: "Cards are also a poor choice when users need to compare between multiple options, since cards often aren't structured in a predictable way from item to item".
2. "eyetracking shows ... re-visit the same items repeatedly" — verbatim: "our eyetracking research revealed that users look back and forth multiple times between items when they compare them"; gaze-plot caption: "Note that the user looks back and forth between the same stories repeatedly, comparing between options before clicking."
3. "does not encode an order ... semirandom" — verbatim caption: "The flexible-card layout does not clearly indicate a hierarchy of stories in order, so the user looks around back and forth in a semirandom pattern".
4. "relative to consistently-positioned list rows" — verbatim: "The irregular layout makes this comparison behavior a more difficult undertaking than a vertical list, in which similar information would be located in pre[dictable locations]" and "Card layouts are less scannable than lists. A standard vertical list view ... is more scannable than cards because the positioning of the individual elements is fixed in size and more predictable for the eye."

DEFECTS FOUND (qualify, do not kill):
(a) "raising cognitive load" is the claimant's wording — "cognitive load" NEVER appears in the article (only "cognitive psychology", re: common regions). NN/g says "a more difficult undertaking" / "less scannable". No cognitive-load instrument (NASA-TLX, pupillometry) was used. Downgrade to "harder / less scannable" or flag as inference.
(b) "eyetracking shows" oversells the evidence: the published artifact is ONE illustrative gaze plot of a single user ("a user's eyetracking session ... she/her"), and the generalization is sourced only to "our eyetracking research" — unpublished, no n, no method, no peer review, no citation in the article. It is authoritative practitioner research, not a controlled study.
(c) Minor task conflation: the gaze-plot task was exploratory ("asked to find and read a story that looked interesting to her"), not a prescribed comparison task, though the caption reports comparison behavior emerging within it.
(d) Age: 2016 core, reviewed 2024. Acceptable — the finding is perceptual/positional (predictable element position aids serial scanning), which is durable; the article itself argues durability of interaction principles. Card grids remain ubiquitous, so it is not stale in application.

NOT refuted: correct primary source, author-attributed, org still maintains it, claim strength ≈ source strength. Usable in STYLES.md/CRAFT.md as the documented "Fails" for card-grid indexes, provided (a) and (b) are reworded.

result.evidence:
The mechanics are quoted accurately, but the claim's STRENGTH FRAMING ("normative W3C/WAI keyboard contract ... has to satisfy") is false, and the absolute "neither key may move focus outside the dialog" is contradicted by W3C's own normative layer and by the platform-native implementation.

1) QUOTE CHECK — accurate. I downloaded https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/ and extracted the text myself: "Tab: Moves focus to the next tabbable element inside the dialog. If focus is on the last tabbable element inside the dialog, moves focus to the first tabbable element inside the dialog"; "Like non-modal dialogs, modal dialogs contain their tab sequence. That is, Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog." So the described behavior is genuinely APG's stated pattern. That part survives.

2) "NORMATIVE" IS WRONG. Grepping the downloaded page: 0 occurrences of "normative", 0 of "Standards Track", 0 conformance language. The APG self-describes as a guide — "How to build accessibility semantics into web patterns and widgets ... It provides design patterns and functional examples complemented by in-depth guidance" (apg home). It is not a W3C Recommendation and defines no conformance requirements. The actual normative W3C keyboard requirement is WCAG SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap, which requires ESCAPABILITY, not cyclic wrapping: "If keyboard focus can be moved to a component ... then focus can be moved away from that component using only a keyboard interface." Cycling is described there as a permitted example, not an obligation: "There may be times when it's appropriate for a web page to restrict focus to a subsection of the content – for example, when the user is inside a modal dialog or popover. This does not fail the requirements of this criterion, as long as the user knows how to 'untrap' the focus."

3) DIRECT CONTRADICTION OF THE ABSOLUTE. WCAG 2.2 Understanding 2.1.2 (w3.org, primary, downloaded verbatim) explicitly blesses focus leaving the dialog: "When the dialog is open, focus is trapped within the dialog – tabbing from the last control in the dialog takes focus to the first control in the dialog (though, depending on implementation, THE FOCUS CYCLE MIGHT STILL INCLUDE USER AGENT CONTROLS)." Focus reaching browser chrome is therefore conformant, which falsifies "neither key may move focus outside the dialog" as a hard requirement.

4) THE RECOMMENDED PLATFORM IMPLEMENTATION VIOLATES THE CLAIM'S LETTER. MDN's <dialog> page recommends showModal() and states the inert-outside behavior "is provided by the browser". Native showModal() does NOT wrap last->first inside the dialog. Scott O'Hara (ARIA/HTML spec editor, TPGi), verbatim from https://www.scottohara.me/blog/2019/03/05/open-dialog.html: "unlike many custom modal dialogs which typically create a focus trap – forcing an endless loop of the focusable elements within the dialog – a native modal <dialog> allows keyboard focus to escape the modal and return to the browser's chrome (e.g., the address bar and other such controls). This is good behavior, not a bug." So a modal built the way the platform and MDN recommend fails the claim as written while being accessible and WCAG-conformant. Note also the APG dialog page never mentions the native dialog element or the inert attribute in the modern sense (only aria-hidden/aria-modal legacy guidance) — it is behind the platform on this point.

5) SCOPE OVERREACH. "any drawer, sheet, side panel or bottom sheet declared modal has to satisfy" — APG's pattern applies to role=dialog/alertdialog; extending it as a universal obligation to every drawer/sheet compounds the normativity error. Platform HIGs (Material bottom sheets, iOS sheets) rely on native modal presentation + inert, i.e. containment, not JS last->first wrapping.

CORRECT RESTATEMENT (usable for the report): normative requirement = WCAG 2.1.2 (focus must be escapable by keyboard; Esc is the standard exit). Recommended practice = ARIA APG dialog pattern (containment, initial focus placement, focus restore on close). Containment is required for a modal; a JS cyclic wrap is ONE way to achieve it and is superseded by <dialog>.showModal() + browser-managed inert, where focus legitimately passes through browser UI.
